q: What do Herman Ebbinghaus, Francis Galton and Sigmund Freud share in common?
who: Ebbinghaus, Galton and Freud, late nineteenth-century pioneers

concept.t: Two separate claims, (a) and (c), are each fully true of all three men, and stopping at one undersells what they share.
All three belong to the late nineteenth-century emergence of psychology as a science, when the study of mind broke away from pure philosophy and physiology and began to use real methods.

Hermann Ebbinghaus (Germany, memory research), Francis Galton (England, differential psychology) and Sigmund Freud (Austria, psychoanalysis) worked in different countries and traditions and never collaborated. Yet each launched a brand-new line of inquiry on his own initiative.

None merely speculated. Ebbinghaus created the nonsense-syllable technique, with himself as sole subject, to chart the forgetting curve, bringing Wilhelm Wundt's experimental rigour to memory; Galton measured individual differences (questionnaires, twin studies, mental tests, correlation), seeding psychometrics and behaviour genetics; Freud used free association and dream interpretation to probe the unconscious, opening the dynamic/clinical tradition parallel to the academic labs.
When two single options are each independently true and a 'both' choice exists, the 'both' choice usually wins, so never stop at the first correct-looking answer.

wrong.a: True of all three (independent, pioneering originality), but only half of what they share: it ignores (c)'s equally true point about new observational methods. True but incomplete, so (d) is the complete answer.
wrong.b: Founding a formal lab belongs to Wilhelm Wundt (first lab, Leipzig in 1879), the standard distractor. None of the three did: Hermann Ebbinghaus self-experimented, Galton ran an anthropometric measurement station, Sigmund Freud worked clinically.
wrong.c: Fully true of all three (nonsense syllables, correlation, free association), but it covers only their methodological side and leaves out (a)'s independent pioneering, so the combined (d) is more complete.

q: In which year the first mental hospital in the USA was opened?
who: Pennsylvania Hospital, Philadelphia, backed by Benjamin Franklin (1753)

concept.t: In 1753 the Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia, the first hospital in the United States, opened its doors and admitted patients with mental illness from the very start.

In the colonial era there was no organised system of care: people with mental illness were confined at home, jailed or left to wander. No public institution received them, and madness was explained in moral and supernatural rather than medical terms.

1753 opens the institutional and moral-treatment story, the move from neglect toward treatment, that later runs through Philippe Pinel 'unchaining' patients in France, William Tuke's York Retreat in England and Dorothea Dix's mid-nineteenth-century reform crusade across America.

Championed by Benjamin Franklin and physician Thomas Bond, it cared for the sick poor of all kinds, and several of its earliest patients were mentally ill. So organised care began inside a general hospital; purpose-built facilities such as the Williamsburg asylum (1773), often called the first American hospital solely for the mentally ill, came later.
First U.S. hospital equals 1753, Philadelphia, with mental patients among its first admissions: a general hospital, not the later dedicated asylums.

wrong.a: Far too early: the American colonies had no public hospital of any kind then, and care of the mentally ill was entirely informal (home confinement or jail). A near-miss late-seventeenth-century decoy.
wrong.c: A real Philadelphia date, but it marks the catastrophic yellow-fever epidemic, not a hospital founding: right city, wrong event. The Pennsylvania Hospital had already been open forty years by then.
wrong.d: The year London's Bethlem Hospital (the infamous 'Bedlam') was granted to the City and became a dedicated asylum, in England, not the USA. Famous, but an English date: wrong by country.

q: Who established the first laboratory for experimental study of psychology?
who: Wilhelm Wundt, Leipzig laboratory (1879)

concept.t: Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory devoted to the experimental study of psychology, conventionally treated as the founding moment of psychology as an independent science.

The mind belonged to two parent disciplines: philosophy, reasoning from the armchair, and physiology, studying the body's sensory and nervous machinery (Weber, Fechner, Helmholtz). No separate discipline examined mental processes through controlled experiment.

Wundt fused the two at the University of Leipzig in 1879, Germany, measuring conscious experience under controlled conditions: timing reactions to stimuli (mental chronometry) and training observers to report sensations by introspection.

With students (Edward Titchener, Hall, Cattell and others) who carried the method across Europe and America, he is the father of experimental psychology; his school is structuralism, later systematised by Titchener. He is the hinge between pre-scientific philosophy of mind and the later schools (functionalism, behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis, the cognitive era), each defined by agreeing with or revolting against his programme.
Lock the trio: Wundt, 1879, Leipzig. For who founded the first psychology lab or made psychology experimental, answer Wundt, not the physiologists or differential-psychology figures around him.

wrong.a: Francis Galton, same era: mental testing, individual differences, an 'anthropometric laboratory' (a tempting word-match). But that was a measurement station gathering public data, not an experimental lab for consciousness, and came after Leipzig.
wrong.b: Ernst Weber, a physiologist: his sensory thresholds (Weber's law, the just-noticeable difference) fed experimental psychology. However, he studied sensation as physiology and founded no psychology lab; he is a precursor to Wilhelm Wundt.
wrong.d: Carl Jung, a psychoanalyst who founded analytical psychology in the early twentieth century. Born 1875, only four years before the Leipzig lab, he worked in the clinical/depth tradition and founded no experimental laboratory.

q: American Psychological Association (APA) was founded in:
who: G. Stanley Hall, Clark University (July 1892)

concept.t: The American Psychological Association was founded in July 1892 at Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts, when a small group of psychologists met to create a national society advancing psychology as a science and profession.

G. Stanley Hall was its driving force and first president. He studied in Wundt's Leipzig tradition, opened one of the first U.S. psychology labs (Johns Hopkins), founded the first American psychology journal and trained many early psychologists.

American psychology came of age and detached from philosophy and physiology. The science born in Wundt's Leipzig lab in 1879 had crossed the Atlantic; William James had published Principles of Psychology (1890); structuralism and emerging functionalism competed; labs multiplied on American campuses.

Practitioners needed a shared organisation for standards, communication and annual meetings. The APA filled that role, marking psychology's professional, institutional phase, and is now the largest professional psychology body in the world.
Lock in APA, 1892, Clark University, Hall as first president. Watch the year: do not blur the founding with later annual meetings, the first formal convention or later expansions.

wrong.b: A deliberate off-by-one decoy next to the true year, catching anyone who recalls 'early 1890s' but not the exact digit. The APA was founded in 1892; the one-year gap is the whole trap.
wrong.c: The year Lightner Witmer opened the first psychological clinic (University of Pennsylvania), launching clinical psychology. A real 'first', but a different one from the APA founding.
wrong.d: Five years after the 1892 founding, a later year offered to muddy the timeline. There is no major APA-founding event in 1897; it only catches those unsure whether it was the early or late 1890s.

q: What is true about Structuralism?
who: Wundt and Titchener's structuralism

concept.t: The signature ambition of structuralism was a mental equivalent of chemistry's periodic table, cataloguing the basic elements of sensation.
Founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory and systematised by his English-born American student Edward Titchener, it was the first formal school after psychology became a science.

As complex substances reduce to a finite set of chemical elements, complex conscious experience should reduce to irreducible mental elements: sensations, images and affective feelings. Disciplined observers isolated them by trained introspection, reporting the raw contents of awareness (quality, intensity, duration) under controlled conditions. The aim was analytic and descriptive: dissect consciousness into atoms and arrange them in an orderly table.

Historically this was psychology's first attempt to look like a hard science. It was challenged by functionalism (what the mind is for, not what it is made of), then largely swept aside by behaviourism, which rejected the study of consciousness; its failure (introspective reports proved unreliable and irreproducible between laboratories) helped trigger both.

Structuralists did care about consciousness generally, but the question rewards the unique goal: reducing consciousness to elemental sensations. So (a) beats the vaguer (b), and the behaviourist-flavoured (c) is simply wrong.

wrong.b: Loosely true, a 'safe' choice, but too broad: it describes the general territory, not structuralism's distinctive aim, the 'periodic table of sensations' in (a). Nor can it fold into 'all the above', since (c) is false.
wrong.c: That is behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), which rejected introspection and consciousness: the opposite of structuralism, which studied the mind by introspection. Studying behaviour alone is false here, and that falsity also sinks (d).
wrong.d: Only correct if every bundled statement is true, and (c) (behaviour not mind) flatly contradicts structuralism. One false member kills an 'all of the above' choice.

q: According to John Dewey, ____ is the connection between sensory stimuli and motor responses.
who: John Dewey, The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology (1896)

concept.t: In his 1896 paper The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology, John Dewey took the reflex arc, the supposed connection between sensory stimulus and motor response, as his explicit subject and target of criticism.

In physiology, a stimulus excites a sensory (afferent) pathway that connects through the nervous system to a motor (efferent) pathway, producing a response; it is usually drawn as a one-way stimulus-then-response chain.

The paper is a founding statement of American functionalism (the Chicago school) and an early shot against stimulus-response (S-R) psychology, which would harden into behaviourism under John B. Watson. S-R treated stimulus and response as separate basic building blocks stitched together.

That carving is artificial: sensation and movement are phases of one continuous, coordinated act of adaptation, and the response loops back to reshape how the next stimulus is perceived (the child reaching for the candle flame is one organised act). Physiology implies a unity of coordinated action, which the old psychology wrongly split. This stress on the whole adaptive act, function over fixed elements, makes the paper functionalist and a bridge toward organism-centred and Gestalt-flavoured thinking.
The term Dewey defined and then criticised is the reflex arc; his contribution was rejecting its fragmentation in favour of a unified, functional act.

wrong.a: Only the outgoing motor limb (efferent: carrying signals away from the centre toward the muscles), so it sounds plausible. John Dewey discussed the whole afferent-to-efferent loop; picking the half-term misses it.
wrong.c: Not a term John Dewey used; there is no such structure in his reflex-arc paper. It borrows the respectable word 'association' (from associationist psychology) to fake a technical concept: a pure fabrication distractor.
wrong.d: Not a recognised Dewey concept either. It appeals because John Dewey argued the act is dynamic and continuous, not static, so the examiner turns his spirit into a plausible false label; he named the reflex arc.

q: According to Titchener, Introspection is a highly specialised form of ______ in which the psychologist attempts to study his own consciousness scientifically.
who: Edward Titchener, structuralist introspection

concept.t: Edward Titchener framed introspection as a highly specialised form of self-observation in which the psychologist studies his own consciousness scientifically.

Wundt's English-born student, he carried German laboratory psychology to America and founded structuralism at Cornell in the 1890s. Its aim, inherited from Wundt's 1879 Leipzig programme, was to reduce mental life to elemental sensations, images and affective states.

Reaching those elements needs a disciplined inward look, not watching behaviour from outside: a comparatively neutral, systematic act of observing the self, unlike casual everyday reflection. Trained observers ('reagents') reported an experience's quality, intensity, duration and clearness, avoiding the stimulus error: naming the object ('an apple') instead of the bare sensation ('a round red patch with these brightness and hue qualities').

Historically this method was structuralism's fatal vulnerability: it proved unreliable and irreproducible, with different labs reporting different 'elements'. That let behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913) dismiss it as unscientific and shift psychology to observable behaviour.

Titchener's introspection is self-observation made rigorous, a controlled report of conscious contents rather than ordinary thinking, perceiving or merely attending. So the answer is self observation, not attention, self-perception or self-thinking.

wrong.a: The term from Daryl Bem's 1960s self-perception theory (we infer our attitudes by observing our behaviour), a social-psychology concept from another era. Edward Titchener's method directly reported the contents of consciousness instead.
wrong.b: Not a recognised term in structuralism's account of introspection, just a loose echo of an inward act. Edward Titchener set his method apart from ordinary thinking, which is itself a conscious content to be observed.
wrong.c: A real, central topic in early experimental psychology (focusing consciousness on a stimulus), but it is an object of study the observer reports on, not the act of self-observation Edward Titchener called introspection.

q: The aim of Functionalism was to study ______ as it functions in adapting the ______ to its environment.
who: William James, Dewey and Angell's functionalism

concept.t: The classic aim of functionalism was to study the mind as it functions in adapting the organism to its environment.

Structuralism (Wundt's Leipzig lab, Titchener at Cornell), the first force, asked what the mind is made of, breaking consciousness into elemental sensations by introspection. Functionalism, the distinctively American second force, led in spirit by William James at Harvard and developed by John Dewey and James Angell at the University of Chicago around the turn of the twentieth century, asked what it is for.

Charles Darwin's evolution drove the shift: if every biological feature aids survival, mental processes (perceiving, remembering, feeling, willing) must serve an adaptive purpose too. The guiding question became practical and biological: how do mental processes help a living creature meet the demands of its surroundings and survive?

So the mind is what is studied and the organism is what it serves. This imported Darwinian thinking into psychology and later seeded evolutionary psychology and applied psychology (education, industry, mental testing).
The order of the blanks is the test: functionalism studies the mind functioning to adapt the organism to its environment, not the reverse.

wrong.a: The right two words in reversed order, the trap for careless readers who skip checking the slots. Making the organism adapt the mind inverts functionalism's logic and its Darwinian, survival-serving role for mental processes.
wrong.c: Too narrow: thinking is one obvious mental activity, but functionalism's declared object was the mind broadly, the whole sweep of mental processes serving adaptation. Substituting one faculty is also historically inaccurate.
wrong.d: Both real terms, but attention is just one specific mental process, not functionalism's overarching subject, and 'individual' does not match the biological framing of an organism adapting to its environment. Both blanks mismatch.

q: ______ of the American Psychological Association represents Health Psychology.
who: APA Division 38, Society for Health Psychology

concept.t: Division 38 of the APA is designated for Health Psychology, now formally called the Society for Health Psychology.

The American Psychological Association (founded 1892, the institutional milestone in psychology becoming a profession) is split into numbered divisions, each a distinct specialty or interest area. The numbers roughly track chartering order, not importance, so they are essentially arbitrary labels.

The psychological side of physical health and illness: how behaviour, stress, beliefs and emotions affect the onset and course of disease, how to promote healthy behaviour, and how psychologists work in healthcare to prevent, treat and manage illness and disability.

Health psychology emerged in the 1970s alongside behavioural medicine. It rests on George Engel's biopsychosocial model (1977): health and illness arise from biological, psychological and social factors together, a direct challenge to the older purely biomedical model it helped overturn. The APA recognises clinical health psychology as a professional specialty, with Division 38 as its organisational home.
A pure memory item: Division 38 equals Health Psychology. Anchor 38 firmly and do not let it slide into the neighbouring numbered divisions.

wrong.a: The Division of School Psychology, serving children and education systems. A real, well-known division, hence a strong decoy, but it has nothing to do with physical health and illness.
wrong.c: The Society for Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology. Exercise and fitness feel close to 'health', but this distinct division focuses on athletic performance, not the biopsychosocial study of illness (Division 38).
wrong.d: A pure fabrication: no APA division numbered that high represents health psychology. The large, round-feeling number catches anyone without firm recall who gambles high; the real designation is Division 38.

q: Which of the following historical perspectives gave rise to the evolutionary perspective?
who: William James and the Chicago school's functionalism

concept.t: The evolutionary perspective grew directly out of functionalism's central question: what mental processes are for.

Founded in spirit by William James and developed by the Chicago school (John Dewey, Angell), it arose in late-nineteenth-century America against structuralism. Where structuralism dissected the contents of consciousness, functionalism, shaped by Charles Darwin's evolution, asked how consciousness helps an organism adapt and survive, putting adaptation, purpose and survival value at the heart of explanation.

A modern perspective that crystallised in the late twentieth century (Tooby, Cosmides, Buss), it explains behaviours and mental traits as products of natural selection: how a tendency improved survival and reproduction in ancestral environments. The bridge is function and adaptive value, which it reframes as inherited, gene-based adaptations.

Structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) catalogued what consciousness contains; psychoanalysis (Freud) used unconscious drives and childhood conflict; behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) used stimulus-response links learned from the environment in a single lifetime. None put inherited adaptive function at the centre.
Functionalism, with its Darwinian adaptive emphasis, seeded the modern evolutionary perspective.

wrong.a: Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) studied conditioned responses and banned inner states and adaptive 'purpose'. Biological-sounding and scientific, but its environment-driven learning opposes the evolutionary stress on inherited, naturally selected traits.
wrong.b: Structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener) catalogued elemental sensations and ignored purpose, function and survival value: the opposite of adaptive thinking. It provoked functionalism as a reaction rather than seeding the evolutionary view.
wrong.c: Psychoanalysis (Freud) explored unconscious drives, childhood conflict and instinctual energy; 'instinct' makes it feel biological. But it explains behaviour by intrapsychic conflict and developmental history, not naturally selected adaptive function.

q: Who is the most associated with the techniques of introspection?
who: Wilhelm Wundt, Leipzig laboratory (1879)

concept.t: Wilhelm Wundt made introspection the signature method of the first scientific psychology, so he is the figure most identified with it.

Not casual self-reflection but a trained, controlled, almost experimental procedure (experimental self-observation). Observers got a precise, repeatable stimulus and reported the immediate contents of consciousness (quality, intensity, duration) under standardised lab conditions, with trials repeated to check reliability.

Wundt founded the first psychology lab at the University of Leipzig in 1879, Germany, psychology's birth as a science, and built structuralism around this method, breaking experience into elements on analogy with chemistry. His student Edward Titchener carried it to America and refined it (the stimulus error), but Wundt is its originator.

William James (functionalism) was sceptical of rigid introspection; John Watson (behaviourism, 1913) rejected it as unscientific, demanding observable behaviour; Max Wertheimer (Gestalt) studied whole perceptual forms. Indeed, introspection's unreliability between labs gave behaviourism its opening.
Wundt, introspection, the Leipzig 1879 lab and structuralism form one cluster: when introspection is named, default to Wundt.

wrong.b: William James, same generation, used and discussed introspection, but founded functionalism and criticised Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener's rigid, element-hunting version, preferring a naturalistic study of the 'stream of consciousness'.
wrong.c: John Watson is linked to introspection for the opposite reason: his 1913 behaviourist manifesto rejected it as unscientific and unverifiable, demanding observable behaviour. Choosing him reverses the relationship; he is its great opponent.
wrong.d: Max Wertheimer founded Gestalt psychology, which studied whole perceptual organisations ('the whole is greater than the sum of its parts') and reacted against the atomistic, element-by-element approach introspection served.

q: Which among the following branches of Psychology specifically studies behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance?
who: Darwin-based evolutionary psychology (Cosmides, Tooby, Buss)

concept.t: Evolutionary psychology is the branch that specifically explains behaviour in relation to genetic inheritance and the action of natural selection.

It applies Charles Darwin's nineteenth-century theory of evolution to the mind, treating psychological traits as products of the selection pressures our ancestors faced. Conceptually it descends from functionalism (William James, Chicago school), which first asked what mental processes are for; it grounded that in genetics, crystallising in the late twentieth century through Leda Cosmides, John Tooby and David Buss.

Tendencies that improved survival and reproduction passed down through the genes, so present-day behaviour carries inherited adaptations from the ancestral 'environment of evolutionary adaptedness'. Fusing psychology with biology, it asks why an emotion, mate preference or fear exists by reconstructing the adaptive problem it solved: ancestral environment, then naturally selected genes, then an inherited tendency.
Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan, health psychology studies behaviour and illness, and experimental psychology names a method, not a content area.
When a question ties behaviour to genes, heredity or natural selection, the answer is evolutionary psychology: heredity and adaptation are its defining lens.

wrong.b: Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan, infancy to old age, and touches genes via nature-nurture. But it weighs nature and nurture over time; 'in relation to genetic inheritance' points to evolutionary psychology.
wrong.c: Health psychology studies how stress, behaviour and beliefs affect physical health and illness, using the biopsychosocial model. 'Biology' makes it feel gene-related, but it is about health behaviour and illness, not inherited traits.
wrong.d: Experimental psychology is defined by its method (controlled laboratory experiments), usable on memory, perception, learning and more, not by any subject matter. It sounds rigorous, but choosing it confuses a methodology with a content focus.

q: Which among the following Schools of Thought used Introspection as a method of analysis?
who: Wundt and Titchener's structuralism

concept.t: Structuralism is the school of thought built on introspection as its method of analysis.

Founded by Wilhelm Wundt in his 1879 Leipzig laboratory, when psychology became an independent science, and systematised by his English-born student Edward Titchener at Cornell, it was the first formal school. Its chemistry-borrowed aim was to reduce mental life to basic elements (sensations, images, affective feelings), like a periodic table of the mind.

You cannot reach those elements by watching behaviour from outside; you must look inward in a disciplined way. Introspection gave a trained, systematic report of one's raw conscious contents under controlled conditions, describing bare qualities (intensity, duration, quality) rather than the object that caused them, so avoiding the stimulus error.

Behaviourism (John B. Watson, around 1913) rejected introspection as unscientific; functionalism (James, John Dewey) used broader observation and applied work; psychoanalysis (Freud) used free association and dream analysis to reach the unconscious. Indeed, introspection's unreliability between labs discredited structuralism and opened the door to behaviourism.
Introspection is the structuralist tool: when a question pairs a school with introspection, choose structuralism.

wrong.a: Functionalism (James, John Dewey), same era, also studied consciousness, but asked what it is for in adaptation and used varied methods (naturalistic observation, mental testing, applied work) rather than strict laboratory introspection.
wrong.b: Behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) is famous for rejecting introspection: Watson called it unscientific and studied observable behaviour alone. Choosing it reverses the relationship; it is introspection's chief opponent.
wrong.d: Psychoanalysis (Freud) used inward-looking clinical techniques, free association and dream analysis, to uncover the unconscious: a depth approach quite unlike controlled laboratory introspection on conscious sensory elements.

q: Who among the following is credited with the book titled Principles of Psychology?
who: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890)

concept.t: William James wrote the landmark two-volume The Principles of Psychology, published in 1890.

Psychology was born in 1879 in Wundt's Leipzig lab and crossed the Atlantic within a decade; James, at Harvard, became its leading American voice. Trained first as a physician before turning to physiology, psychology and philosophy, he set up an early demonstration lab in the United States and inspired functionalism (what the mind is for), a Darwinian counterweight to the structuralism of Wilhelm Wundt and Titchener.

A synthesis of more than a decade of his thinking, it became the foundational American textbook of the discipline, shaping generations; it was so vast that he later issued a condensed version, nicknamed 'Jimmy'.

It introduced the stream of consciousness (experience as a continuous flowing whole, challenging the structuralists' sensory atoms), habit as the 'flywheel of society', the James-Lange theory of emotion (we feel afraid because we tremble, not the reverse) and a pioneering treatment of the self. These made James the bridge between the new laboratory science and a broader, practical, biologically minded psychology.

Lock the link: James, The Principles of Psychology, 1890. Take care not to credit Wundt, whose similar text was Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873-74); the English Principles of Psychology is James's.

wrong.a: Wilhelm Wundt wrote Principles of Physiological Psychology, an almost identical title the examiner exploits. But it has the extra word 'Physiological' and is structuralist/experimental; the plain Principles of Psychology (1890) is William James's.
wrong.c: B.F. Skinner belongs to a later era and behaviourism; his works were on operant conditioning, such as The Behavior of Organisms (1938) and Science and Human Behavior. He wrote no Principles of Psychology.
wrong.d: Wrong because William James clearly and famously wrote The Principles of Psychology in 1890; with a correct named author among the options, the catch-all cannot be right.

q: Who among the following was the first female president of the American Psychological Association (APA)?
who: Mary Whiton Calkins, first female APA president (1905)

concept.t: Mary Whiton Calkins was the first woman to serve as president of the American Psychological Association, taking office as its 14th president in 1905.

At the turn of the twentieth century American psychology, fresh from Wundt's Leipzig revolution, was institutionalising itself through the APA (founded 1892), university labs and doctoral programmes, almost entirely under men.

She studied under William James (the functionalist) and Hugo Munsterberg at Harvard and completed every doctoral requirement; James reportedly called her examination the finest he had seen. Yet Harvard refused her the degree because she was a woman.

Despite that, she invented the paired-associate technique for memory (items learned in pairs so one cues recall of the other, still used today), ran one of the first psychology labs at a women's college (Wellesley), and built a systematic psychology of the self anticipating later self and personality theory. Her 1905 election broke the gender barrier at the top of organised American psychology, a milestone comparable in symbolic weight to the field's founding firsts.

First female APA president equals Calkins, 1905. Do not confuse her with Margaret Floy Washburn: first woman psychology PhD (1894, under Edward Titchener), and in 1921 the second female APA president.

wrong.a: The twin-trap: the first woman to earn a psychology PhD (1894), and an APA president, but only the second woman to be one, in 1921. The first female president was Calkins (1905).
wrong.b: A genuine pioneer in the psychology of women (debunking 'variability' myths) and of gifted children, but never APA president. She rewards partial knowledge of early women in the field while still being wrong.
wrong.c: A famous neo-Freudian in the psychoanalytic tradition, challenging Freud on feminine psychology, working largely in Germany and then the USA as a clinician and theorist. She never served as APA president.

q: Given below are two statements, first labelled assertion (A) and the other labelled as reason (R). Indicate your answer using the codes given below: Assertion (A): Fritz perls was a proponent of the gestalt perspective. Reason (R): Gestalt focuses on the wholeness of individuals' experiences in the present moment.
who: Fritz Perls, with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman, Gestalt therapy

concept.t: Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion: present-moment wholeness is exactly why Fritz Perls is classed as Gestalt rather than simply humanistic.
Perls, together with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman, founded Gestalt therapy in the mid-twentieth century, so he was a proponent of the Gestalt perspective.

Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Kohler) began as a theory of perception: 'the whole is more than the sum of its parts', with experience organised into meaningful wholes. Historically it arose in early-twentieth-century Germany as a reaction against the atomism of structuralism.

Perls transplanted this principle into therapy: present-moment awareness, the here-and-now, and integrating fragmented parts of the self, rather than excavating the past as psychoanalysis did. Trained in psychoanalysis before breaking from it, he carried wholeness into the humanistic 'third force' of the 1950s and 60s, alongside Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow.

Gestalt therapy is often loosely grouped with humanistic-existential approaches, but wholeness-in-the-present marks it as Gestalt, so R is the criterion for A, not an incidental truth. When both are true and R states the principle justifying A, R is the correct explanation.

wrong.b: Keeps both true but denies the link, as if they were two unrelated facts. Present-moment wholeness is not a coincidental fact about Gestalt but the very reason Perls counts as Gestalt, not just humanistic.
wrong.c: R is not false: present-moment wholeness accurately describes the Gestalt approach. This baits anyone who doubts the 'here-and-now wholeness' characterisation, which is precisely correct.
wrong.d: A is firmly true: Fritz Perls founded Gestalt therapy. This tempts students who wrongly file Perls under humanistic or existential psychology, but his core identity is Gestalt.

q: Herman von Helmholtz (1821-94):
who: Hermann von Helmholtz, Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory

concept.t: Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) is credited with developing the trichromatic theory of colour vision.

The eye must encode a vast range of colours from light. Building on Thomas Young (hence the Young-Helmholtz theory), it holds that colour vision rests on three types of cones, each most sensitive to short, medium or long wavelengths (roughly blue, green, red); any colour arises from their relative activation, so three primaries can reproduce the visible spectrum. Ewald Hering's opponent-process theory later complemented it at a different stage of the visual system.

He was a nineteenth-century physician-physicist of the physiological tradition, the parent discipline that, with philosophy, gave birth to scientific psychology in 1879. With Weber, Fechner and Muller he was a pre-Wundt precursor whose precise sensory measurement showed mental and neural processes could be quantified, making an experimental psychology conceivable.

Beyond colour, he was the first to measure the speed of nerve conduction, showing it is finite and measurable rather than instantaneous. That opened the study of reaction time and mental chronometry, running from Wilhelm Wundt's lab to modern cognitive psychology.
Helmholtz equals the trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) theory, three cone types. Do not attach the just-noticeable difference (Weber and Fechner) or the law of effect (Edward Thorndike) to him.

wrong.a: The jnd and Weber's law belong to Ernst Weber and Gustav Fechner, founders of psychophysics. All three were nineteenth-century German sensory scientists, so contributions get swapped; Helmholtz's signature is colour vision and nerve speed.
wrong.c: The unconscious is Sigmund Freud's construct (with roots in Schopenhauer and Hartmann). Helmholtz did write about 'unconscious inference' in perception, but that narrow idea is not the Freudian dynamic unconscious meant here.
wrong.d: Edward Thorndike's law from his puzzle-box experiments: satisfying consequences strengthen responses. A cornerstone of learning theory from another era and tradition (American connectionism/behaviourism), unrelated to Helmholtz's colour vision.

q: Which one of the following branches of philosophy of science deals with the question of existence?
who: Ontology, the study of being

concept.t: Among the branches of the philosophy of science, ontology is the one that deals with the question of existence.

The branch of metaphysics concerned with what exists, the nature of being, and the kinds and structures of entities that make up reality. From the Greek ontos (being) and logos (study), it asks what sorts of things exist, how they are categorised and what it means to be real.

Epistemology (from episteme, knowledge) asks instead how we can know reality and what counts as valid knowledge. In research methodology the two found every paradigm and shape method choice: your ontological stance concerns the reality studied (one objective reality, the realist view, or a socially constructed one, the relativist view); your epistemological stance, how you can know it.

The pairing underlies the split in the human sciences between positivist research (objective reality, measured experimentally) and interpretivist research (constructed meaning, understood qualitatively), running through psychology's century-long debate about imitating the natural sciences.

Post-positivism and scientific realism are positions within the philosophy of science (largely epistemological or metaphysical stances), and structuralism is a school of thought. Existence and being equal ontology; knowing equals epistemology.

wrong.a: The successor to positivism: it accepts an external reality but holds our knowledge of it is always fallible and theory-laden. That is an epistemological stance (how we know), not a branch studying what exists.
wrong.b: In psychology, Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener's school analysing the structure of consciousness; in linguistics/anthropology, a separate movement. Either way a school or method, not a branch about being: a familiar-word trap.
wrong.d: The position that successful scientific theories truly describe a mind-independent world, unobservables included. It touches existence, a clever trap, but it is a stance on whether theories track reality, not the branch studying being.

q: Who is often referred to as the "Founder of Modern Psychology in India"?
who: Narendra Nath Sen Gupta, University of Calcutta (1916)

concept.t: Narendra Nath Sen Gupta is regarded as the founder of modern psychology in India, having established the country's first independent psychology department.

Scientific psychology was born in Wundt's Leipzig lab in 1879 and spread out from Germany. In India the mind was treated within philosophy and classical speculative traditions (Vedanta, Samkhya, Yoga), with no Western-style experimental discipline.

Trained at Harvard (under figures such as Hugo Munsterberg) in the experimental lab approach, he founded India's first independent department of psychology and first psychology lab at the University of Calcutta in 1916, the Calcutta milieu that would soon host India's psychoanalytic movement. That shift from armchair philosophy to laboratory-based experimental study along Western lines is what 'modern' means in his title.
He co-authored an early Indian psychology textbook with Radhakamal Mukerjee and helped train and work alongside the next generation, including the psychoanalyst Girindra Shekhar Bose.

Lock in Sen Gupta, first department and lab, University of Calcutta, 1916. Take care not to credit M.V. Gopalswamy, who founded the Mysore department and did important applied and experimental work, but later.

wrong.a: The father of psychoanalysis in India, founder of the Indian Psychoanalytic Society and a noted correspondent of Sigmund Freud: foundational, but in a different stream. The first experimental department is Sen Gupta's distinction.
wrong.c: Not a recognised founder of modern Indian psychology; a plausible Bengali-sounding name for those who know the discipline began in Calcutta. There is no documented 'founder' claim attached to it, unlike Sen Gupta's record.
wrong.d: A real pioneer who founded the psychology department at the University of Mysore and advanced applied and experimental psychology in India. But it came after Calcutta's 1916 department, so the founder title is Sen Gupta's.

q: Select the incorrect pair:
who: Jean Piaget's formal operations, not Kohlberg's moral stages

concept.t: Formal operations belongs to Jean Piaget, not Lawrence Kohlberg, whose name is tied to moral development, so this is the incorrect pair.

In the cognitive-developmental tradition (outside the psychodynamic schools, yet tested beside them), Piaget, the Swiss genetic epistemologist, mapped four invariant cognitive stages: sensorimotor (0-2), preoperational (2-7), concrete operational (7-11) and formal operational (roughly 11+), where abstract, hypothetical, propositional reasoning emerges.

At Harvard in the 1950s-70s, Kohlberg applied Piaget's stage logic to moral reasoning: three levels, each split into two stages: preconventional (obedience, self-interest), conventional (approval, law-and-order) and postconventional (social contract, universal ethical principles).

Kohlberg was Piaget's heir; both used hierarchical, sequence-fixed stages driven by qualitative reorganization of thought, so a swap almost looks right. But formal operations is how we think abstractly; Kohlberg's stages are how we judge right and wrong.

Historically the options mix schools: Carl Jung (analytical psychology) and Alfred Adler (individual psychology) split off from Sigmund Freud, and Albert Ellis founded a cognitive-behavioural therapy in the 1950s; only the Kohlberg-Piaget mismatch is broken. Any pairing that gives Kohlberg a Piagetian term is the incorrect pair.

wrong.a: True: Carl Jung, founder of analytical psychology and the most famous Freud defector, coined the introversion-extroversion attitude dimension in Psychological Types (1921). A correct pair cannot be the answer.
wrong.c: True: Alfred Adler, founder of Individual Psychology, described a fourfold typology: the Ruling/Dominant type plus the getting, avoiding and socially useful types. It is less rehearsed than Sigmund Freud's structures, but correct.
wrong.d: True: Albert Ellis founded Rational Emotive Therapy (later REBT) in the 1950s, the first major cognitive therapy. It lures students who confuse Ellis with Aaron Beck, but the link is accurate.

q: Who published the mechanism of hysteria in 1893?
who: Sigmund Freud and Josef Breuer, Preliminary Communication (1893)

concept.t: The 1893 paper on the mechanism of hysteria was the joint work of Sigmund Freud and the senior Viennese physician Josef Breuer, issued as their Preliminary Communication and expanded in 1895 into Studies on Hysteria.

This is the prehistory of psychoanalysis, the moment before Freud's mature system existed, when he was still a neurologist working with an older mentor. Hysteria meant physical symptoms (paralysis, blindness, mutism, fits) with no organic cause; Breuer and Freud argued these were the bodily conversion of repressed emotional trauma.

Breuer's patient Anna O. (Bertha Pappenheim) found her symptoms eased when she traced each one back to the forgotten memory that triggered it; she called this the talking cure or chimney-sweeping, and Breuer labelled it catharsis. The seed claim: 'hysterics suffer mainly from reminiscences', meaning blocked affect, denied normal discharge, converts into symptoms.

The collaboration supplied the raw ideas (the unconscious, repression, cure through verbal recall) that Freud built into psychoanalysis proper before Breuer, uneasy with the sexual emphasis, fell away. Charcot comes before (Freud's 1885-86 Paris training in hypnosis); the great defectors Alfred Adler and Jung come over a decade after, breaking from a theory that did not yet exist in 1893.
The 1893 hysteria work and the Anna O. case belong to Breuer, the bridge figure between hypnosis-era medicine and psychoanalysis.

wrong.a: Jean-Martin Charcot, the great Parisian neurologist at the Salpetriere, taught Freud about hysteria and hypnotic suggestion in 1885-86. He came before the Vienna work and did not co-author the 1893 paper; that was Josef Breuer.
wrong.c: Alfred Adler joined Freud's Wednesday circle only around 1902 and broke away in 1911 to found Individual Psychology. He had no part in the 1890s hysteria studies, which predate his arrival by roughly a decade.
wrong.d: Carl Jung began corresponding with Freud only in 1906 and broke from him by 1913. The most celebrated collaborator-turned-defector, he was a teenager in 1893 and played no part in the hysteria research with Breuer.

q: Reports on sexual behaviour of men was published by
who: Alfred Kinsey, the Kinsey Reports (1948, 1953)

concept.t: The landmark reports on human sexual behaviour were empirical survey works, not theory, produced by Alfred Kinsey and his team at Indiana University.

They sit outside the psychodynamic tradition, in mid-twentieth-century empirical sexology, a deliberate break from the armchair, moralistic and psychoanalytic treatment of sex. Kinsey was a zoologist (originally a gall-wasp taxonomist) who brought large-scale, quantitative biological data-collection to a taboo subject.

Sexual Behaviour in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behaviour in the Human Female (1953) rest on thousands of confidential face-to-face interviews. Co-authors were Wardell Pomeroy, Clyde Martin and (female volume) Paul Gebhard; the publisher was W.B. Saunders.

The Kinsey scale, a 0-to-6 continuum from exclusively heterosexual to exclusively homosexual, reframed orientation as a spectrum rather than two fixed boxes. The data showed behaviours assumed rare were widespread, making the reports scandalous and foundational and helping launch modern sex research, later continued by William Masters and Virginia Johnson.

Theory versus measurement: Sigmund Freud theorized about sexuality from the clinic (libido, psychosexual stages); Kinsey measured it through surveys. Who reported on (counted, surveyed) sexual behaviour is Kinsey, the empiricist, not any psychoanalyst.

wrong.a: The psychoanalyst who made sexuality central (libido, psychosexual stages), but he theorized from individual clinical cases and never produced statistical, interview-based survey reports. 'Reports' signals empirical data: Alfred Kinsey's domain.
wrong.c: Sigmund's daughter, who pioneered child psychoanalysis and systematized the ego defence mechanisms. The famous surname tempts, but her work was defences and child analysis, not large-scale sexual-behaviour surveys.
wrong.d: A neo-Freudian known for basic anxiety and for challenging Freud on feminine psychology (penis envy versus womb envy). She wrote about sex-linked psychology, but produced theory, not survey reports of sexual behaviour.

q: Who is the father of Psychoanalysis?
who: Sigmund Freud, founder of psychoanalysis

concept.t: Sigmund Freud is universally credited as founder of psychoanalysis, the theory and treatment method that defines the first force of depth psychology.

Psychoanalysis is both a model of the mind and a therapy. As a model, the mind is largely unconscious, behaviour is driven by instinctual urges (sexual and aggressive), and personality is structured into id, ego and superego.

It brings repressed unconscious conflicts into awareness through free association, dream interpretation (dreams as the 'royal road to the unconscious') and analysis of resistance and transference. Freud, an Austrian neurologist in Vienna, built this from his 1890s clinical work on hysteria and set out the dream theory in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900).

He is the trunk of the psychodynamic tree: early loyalists, then the great defectors Alfred Adler (Individual Psychology, broke away 1911) and Carl Jung (Analytical Psychology, broke away ~1913), then the neo-Freudians (Karen Horney, Erich Fromm, Harry Stack Sullivan), ego psychologists and object-relations theorists. Every one of those schools is a reaction to Freud, which is why he, not his successors, is 'the father'.

Bernheim was a hypnosis-and-suggestion figure who influenced Freud but founded nothing of the sort; Adler and Jung each founded a rival school under a different name. The single originator of psychoanalysis, the parent theory they all defined themselves against, is Freud.

wrong.a: Hippolyte Bernheim of the Nancy school championed hypnotic suggestion and influenced the young Freud's thinking. He worked in the hypnosis tradition and never created psychoanalysis; he is upstream of it, not its author.
wrong.c: An early member of Freud's circle who broke away in 1911 to found Individual Psychology (social urges, inferiority). Founding a rival school is not founding psychoanalysis, which was Freud's.
wrong.d: Once Freud's anointed heir, he split off around 1913 to found Analytical Psychology (collective unconscious, archetypes). A distinct school; the parent theory of psychoanalysis belongs to Freud alone.

q: Freud published The Interpretation of Dreams in:
who: Sigmund Freud, Die Traumdeutung (dated 1900)

concept.t: 1900 is the official publication date on Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams (Die Traumdeutung).

The book physically appeared in early November 1899, but the Leipzig-Vienna publisher Franz Deuticke post-dated it to 1900 so it would read as heralding the new century. The canonical exam answer is 1900, even though Panwar notes the 4 November 1899 printing.

The founding text of the mature psychoanalytic theory of the unconscious, where Sigmund Freud moved from the hysteria collaboration with Breuer into a system of his own. Core claim: dreams are wish-fulfilments and the 'royal road to the unconscious'. It let him study the unconscious in healthy people, not only patients, and made dream analysis a central pillar of technique.

Manifest content (the dream as consciously remembered) and latent content (the hidden, often forbidden wish) are linked by the dream-work: condensation, displacement and symbolization turn the unacceptable wish into an acceptable image. This is early, pre-structural Freud; the id-ego-superego scheme came later, in 1923.
The book is dated 1900 and its thesis is that dreams are disguised wish-fulfilments. Remembering the dawn-of-the-century post-dating protects you against the 1898 and even 1899 distractors.

wrong.b: Predates the book: in 1898 Freud was still doing the self-analysis and dream-collection that fed it. The writing began in the late 1890s, but the published, dated work is 1900.
wrong.c: Two years too late. 1902 is when Freud gained his professorship and the Wednesday Psychological Society began forming, real milestones, but not the dream book's date.
wrong.d: Four years too late, nearer The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) or later works. A pure distance distractor, plausible only with no anchor for the turn-of-the-century date.

q: Children with organic defects and those born into minority groups are likely to develop ____.
who: Alfred Adler, Individual Psychology

concept.t: In Alfred Adler's Individual Psychology, real disadvantages such as organic defects (bodily weakness or 'organ inferiority') or minority-group marginalization can intensify ordinary inferiority feelings into a chronic, disabling complex.

Adler was the first major defector from Sigmund Freud, breaking away in 1911 to replace the sexual drive with a social, goal-directed psychology. Everyone begins life small, weak and dependent, giving a universal feeling of inferiority that in the healthy case drives striving for superiority (or perfection), the push toward mastery and competence.

When the feeling becomes overwhelming, it hardens into an inferiority complex, a fixed sense of inadequacy that blocks functioning instead of fuelling it. Adler's three childhood risk roots are organ inferiority / physical defect, pampering and neglect; marginalized or minority children fall under the neglected, disadvantaged category because their handicap can feel insurmountable.
The linked idea is compensation and overcompensation, the attempt to offset the weakness, which can mask itself as a superiority complex.

A normal inferiority feeling is universal and motivating; an inferiority complex is the pathological, stuck version. Defect and minority disadvantage point to that complex, not to healthy striving or its overcompensated superiority mask.

wrong.a: Adler's overcompensated mask over deep inferiority, a secondary defence layered on top and causally downstream. What such children 'develop' from their handicap is the inferiority complex itself.
wrong.c: Adler's healthy striving mechanism, the effort to offset a weakness through growth or skill. It names the corrective response, not the disabling deficit state the disadvantage produces.
wrong.d: Adler's fictional finalism: people are pulled forward by an imagined future ideal that guides the style of life. Real Adlerian theory, but about teleological motivation, not how defect or minority status breeds inadequacy.

q: Jung disagreed with Freud on the nature of the unconscious, arguing that it exists on two levels ____ and ____.
who: Carl Jung, Analytical Psychology

concept.t: Carl Jung split the unconscious into a personal (individual) unconscious and a deeper collective unconscious; that second layer is the point on which he broke from Sigmund Freud.

Freud's unconscious is wholly personal: repressed memories and forbidden wishes acquired in one's own lifetime. Jung, Freud's designated heir until their 1913 split that birthed Analytical Psychology, kept that layer as the personal unconscious, holding forgotten and suppressed experiences unique to the person.

Beneath it lies the collective unconscious, inherited and shared by all humanity, a psychic deposit of the species' evolutionary and ancestral history. Its contents are the archetypes, universal predisposing patterns and images (the shadow, the anima/animus, the wise old man, the great mother) that recur across myths, religions and dreams.

Jung's reading of comparative religion, Eastern philosophy (Buddhism, Hinduism) and alchemy shaped this view, which is why Freud, the rationalist, rejected it as mystical. All four options are real Jungian terms, so you must tell the levels from the contents or dimensions.

The personal/individual unconscious is yours alone and acquired in your lifetime; the collective unconscious is universal and inherited. Two levels of the unconscious in Jung means personal/individual and collective.

wrong.b: Archetypes: the inner feminine within a man and the inner masculine within a woman, which reside inside the collective unconscious. They are contents of the deep layer, not its two structural levels.
wrong.c: Jung's two attitude types from Psychological Types (1921), describing the direction of psychic energy. A conscious personality dimension, not divisions of the unconscious.
wrong.d: Echo Jung's psychological functions (thinking, feeling, sensation, intuition) and the later MBTI-style preferences built on him. They describe modes of orienting to the world, not the layered structure of the unconscious.

q: In a psychoanalytic practice, where the patient relaxes on a couch and freely tells whatever comes into his/her mind is called
who: Freud, classical psychoanalytic technique

concept.t: Free association is Freud's defining technique: the patient reclines and reports whatever enters the mind, uncensored.

Psychoanalysis aims to surface repressed material from the unconscious. Direct questioning fails because the patient's defences guard the painful content; free association sidesteps them by having the patient voice every thought, image and feeling as it arises, however trivial, embarrassing, illogical or irrelevant.
It rests on psychic determinism: mental life is never random, so a chain of seemingly stray associations is steered by unconscious conflicts, and following it leads back to the repressed root.

Freud developed free association to replace hypnosis, the cathartic-hypnotic method he took from Charcot in Paris and his colleague Josef Breuer in Vienna; hypnosis was unreliable and made patients parrot the analyst's suggestions, while free association let patients 'speak for themselves'. Points where the patient hesitates, blanks, blushes or changes subject signal resistance, and associations often expose transference.
Couch plus an uncensored stream of thought equals free association, the core royal route (alongside dream interpretation) into the unconscious in classical psychoanalysis.

wrong.a: Links to dream interpretation, the other great psychoanalytic route to the unconscious. But dreaming is a sleeping mental event analysed afterward, not the waking, on-the-couch technique of speaking every thought aloud.
wrong.b: Not a defined psychoanalytic technique, just an everyday word for telling an account. Free association is precisely unstructured and uncensored, the opposite of a coherent narrative.
wrong.d: Not the technical term either: a story is organized, sequenced and edited, whereas free association demands a deliberately disorganized, unedited flow. That absence of structure is what lets repressed links surface.

q: Karen Horney's conception of feelings of pervasive loneliness and helplessness that are the foundation of neurosis is called
who: Karen Horney, neo-Freudian theory of neurosis

concept.t: Karen Horney used exactly the phrase basic anxiety for the pervasive loneliness and helplessness she placed at the foundation of neurosis.

A leading neo-Freudian, trained in psychoanalysis but rejecting Sigmund Freud's biological, libido-and-instinct account in favour of social and relational causes. She also challenged Freud's view of feminine psychology, replacing 'penis envy' with male 'womb envy'.

Basic anxiety arises in childhood when the parent-child environment goes wrong: domination, indifference, erratic or hostile behaviour, lack of respect for the child's individual needs, or no genuine warmth and guidance. The child feels small, isolated and helpless in a potentially hostile world, and this insecure foundation later breeds neurosis.

To cope, the person adopts rigid strategies, the three neurotic trends: moving toward people (compliance, self-effacement, seeking approval), against people (aggression, control, need to dominate) or away from people (detachment, withdrawal). The healthy person uses all three flexibly; the neurotic clings compulsively to one.

'Basic anxiety' is Horney's specific named concept, learned from disturbed early relationships, distinct from Freud's drive-based 'neurotic anxiety' and the philosophers' 'existential anxiety'. Pervasive childhood helplessness as the origin of neurosis, tied to Horney, means basic anxiety.

wrong.a: Not a Horney term; it contradicts her thesis. Karen Horney insisted basic anxiety is learned from childhood interpersonal experience, not biologically inborn; 'innate' is exactly what she argued against.
wrong.b: A concept from existential and humanistic psychology (Rollo May, Irvin Yalom, drawing on Kierkegaard and Heidegger): dread of meaninglessness, freedom and death. A different school, not Horney's foundation-of-neurosis term.
wrong.d: Sigmund Freud's term: the ego's fear that the id's impulses will break through and overwhelm it. The strongest decoy, but drive-based and intrapsychic, not Horney's relationally caused basic anxiety.

q: The Ego is sometimes described as the ____ because it directs energies supplied by the Id.
who: Sigmund Freud, structural model (1923)

concept.t: Freud described the ego as the executive of personality, the agency that directs and manages the psychic energy supplied by the id.

Freud's 1923 structural model is the mature phase of his theory, succeeding the topographical (conscious/unconscious) scheme. The id is the primitive reservoir of instinctual energy demanding immediate gratification on the pleasure principle; the superego is the internalized moral code, conscience plus ego-ideal.

The ego sits between them, faces reality and runs on the reality principle through secondary process thinking: it satisfies the id only in realistic, safe, socially acceptable ways while honouring the superego. Weighing costs and benefits, delaying gratification, testing reality and deciding when and how desires are discharged is an executive function, like a manager allocating resources it does not generate.

The ego has no libido of its own; it borrows energy from the id and channels it, and directing energy it did not produce earns the 'executive' label. Historically this mediator-ego launched the ego psychology school (Anna Freud, Heinz Hartmann, Erik Erikson), which expanded its autonomous, adaptive functions.
The id supplies the drive, the superego supplies the rules, and the ego executes, balancing both against the constraints of reality.

wrong.b: Implies the ego ranks above id and superego. Sigmund Freud's ego does not dominate; it serves and balances three masters (id, superego, reality), often anxiously. 'Executive' means managing, not outranking.
wrong.c: Wrongly demotes the ego to a servile role. It does borrow its energy from the id, but functionally it is the managing, directing structure, so this inverts its actual status.
wrong.d: A Rogerian / humanistic term for the match between self-concept and lived experience, from a completely different school. It has no Freudian meaning for the ego.

q: According to Sigmund Freud, the id operates on
who: Sigmund Freud, the id and the pleasure principle

concept.t: Freud held that the id operates entirely on the pleasure principle.

The oldest, most primitive of the three structures in Freud's structural model, present from birth and wholly unconscious. It houses the instinctual drives (Eros and, later, Thanatos) and is the source of all psychic energy, the libido.

The pleasure principle demands every wishful impulse be satisfied immediately, regardless of consequence, logic, morality or external reality; getting it feels like pleasure, being blocked like rising tension or 'unpleasure' to be discharged at once. The id uses primary process thinking (primitive, illogical, irrational, timeless, fantasy-oriented) and can even hallucinate the desired object (wish-fulfilment) to relieve tension.

The newborn who cries the instant it is hungry is pure id on the pleasure principle, with no capacity to wait. Placing it in the psychodynamic arc, the id-ego-superego triad belongs to Freud's 1923 structural revision and seeds the later ego-psychology tradition.
The id runs on the pleasure principle and primary process; the ego runs on the reality principle and secondary process, delaying gratification to fit the real world.

wrong.b: Governs the ego, the realistic, delaying, consequence-weighing agency, not the id. The strongest decoy as the matched opposite term, but assigning it to the id reverses Sigmund Freud's scheme.
wrong.c: A region or level of the psyche in the topographical model, not a 'principle'. The id genuinely is entirely unconscious, but a location is not the principle it runs on.
wrong.d: Also a level of awareness, not an operating principle, and doubly wrong: the id has no conscious component. It confuses 'where the id lives' with 'how the id works'.

q: According to Sigmund Freud, wars and violence are evidence of
who: Sigmund Freud, Thanatos in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920)

concept.t: Freud interpreted wars and violence as expressions of the death instinct.

This is Freud's late, post-First-World-War dual-instinct theory, a darkening of psychoanalysis after he witnessed mass slaughter. Against the earlier sex-centred picture, Eros, the life instinct, gathers the sexual and self-preservative urges, is fuelled by libido, and binds, builds and sustains life.

Opposed to it stands Thanatos, the death instinct, introduced in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920): 'the goal of all life is death', a pull back toward an earlier, inorganic, tensionless state. Since the organism cannot simply annihilate itself, it is typically turned outward as aggression, cruelty, war and violence; turned inward, it can surface as self-harm, depression, masochism or suicide.

This pessimistic view, deepened in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and his exchange with Einstein on 'Why War?', was controversial and largely rejected by the neo-Freudians and even by Freud's own daughter's ego-psychology successors.

Libido and the life instinct concern preservation, bonding and pleasure; aggression, destruction and war trace to the death instinct (Thanatos). 'Wars and violence' is the textbook signal for it, not Eros or libido.

wrong.a: Eros drives survival, sexuality, bonding and creation, the constructive opposite of the forces behind war. The natural counterpart in the dual-instinct pair, but the wrong pole: Eros builds and unites, war expresses Thanatos.
wrong.b: The energy of Eros, the sexual/life-instinct drive, and Sigmund Freud's most famous energetic term. It fuels the life instinct, not aggression; destructiveness is the work of the death instinct.
wrong.d: Wrong because Freud explicitly attributed aggression and war to the death instinct in Beyond the Pleasure Principle and later works. He plainly committed to a clear answer.

q: Errors in speech that reflect unconscious thoughts or impulses is
who: Sigmund Freud, The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901)

concept.t: Errors of speech that betray unconscious thoughts are exactly what a Freudian slip is.

Sigmund Freud's own technical term is parapraxis (German Fehlleistung): a slip of the tongue, pen or memory that is never random but always meaningful. It rests on psychic determinism: mental life is fully caused, so even a trivial verbal mistake comes from a repressed wish, impulse or thought leaking past the ego's censorship into everyday behaviour.
A person who intends one word but substitutes another tied to what they secretly feel, or who 'forgets' a name linked to an uncomfortable association, has exposed unconscious content.

In The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) Freud treated slips, lapses, bungled actions and forgetting as windows into the unconscious, alongside dreams and jokes as everyday counterparts of the clinical symptom. Placing it historically, this is early-Freud material, the same turn-of-the-century project as the dream book, showing the unconscious works in normal people, not only patients.

A defence mechanism is an unconscious anxiety-management strategy and a cognitive distortion is a faulty thinking pattern from a rival (cognitive) school; neither is specifically a speech error revealing the unconscious. 'Errors in speech reflecting unconscious impulses' means the Freudian slip.

wrong.a: An unconscious ego strategy that wards off anxiety (repression, projection, denial and so on). It is unconscious, but it is a general protective manoeuvre, not specifically a slip of the tongue, which is the parapraxis.
wrong.c: Biased thinking patterns (catastrophizing, all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization) from the cognitive therapy of Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis, a different tradition. Conscious-level reasoning errors, not unconscious verbal leaks.
wrong.d: Stuttering, articulation or fluency impairment: an organic, neurological or developmental condition. A literal-minded decoy; such errors have a physical or developmental cause, not an unconscious psychological one.

q: According to Jung, the archetype representing the feminine side of males is called:
who: Carl Jung, Analytical Psychology

concept.t: In Carl Jung's analytical psychology the anima is the unconscious feminine archetype carried within a man.

Archetypes are universal, inherited patterns in the collective unconscious, the deep stratum shared across humanity that was Jung's great divergence from Sigmund Freud. Among them is a contrasexual pair: every man holds an inner feminine image, the anima, and every woman an inner masculine image, the animus.

It carries a man's unconscious feminine qualities (feeling, relatedness, receptivity, mood, eros) and shapes how he relates to women, often by projection onto a partner, and to his own emotional life. Integrating it is essential to individuation, uniting conscious and unconscious into a balanced, whole Self; a man who denies his anima stays one-sided, prey to moods he cannot own.

The shadow is the repressed, instinctual dark side (loosely like Freud's id); the persona is the social mask presented to meet external demands. Placing Jung historically, he was Freud's heir until their 1913 break founded Analytical Psychology, trading Freud's sexual drive for a symbolic, spiritual, lifelong model of growth.
Anima is the feminine-within-the-male; animus is the masculine-within-the-female. The feminine side of a male is the anima, not the animus.

wrong.a: The exact reverse archetype: the unconscious masculine image within a woman. The strongest decoy, since anima and animus are near-twins differing only by direction; the feminine side of a male is the anima.
wrong.b: The repressed, instinctual, often darker side of the psyche, roughly like Sigmund Freud's id. A core Jungian archetype, but about disowned instinct and 'darkness', not gender.
wrong.c: The social mask worn to satisfy external demands and present an acceptable face to the world. It concerns the public self, not an inner gendered archetype.

q: According to psychoanalytic perspective, the terms gratification, irrational and impulsive are related to:
who: Sigmund Freud, structural model (1923)

concept.t: Gratification, irrationality and impulsiveness are the defining qualities of the id.

The most primitive of Sigmund Freud's three personality structures in the 1923 structural model, wholly unconscious and present from birth. It stores the instinctual drives, supplies all psychic energy (the libido) and runs on the pleasure principle, demanding immediate gratification of every urge regardless of logic, morality, reality or consequence.

Its mode is primary process thinking: irrational, illogical, timeless, impulsive and fantasy-driven, even hallucinating the wished-for object to discharge tension. It has no contact with the external world and cannot tolerate delay, which is why 'gratification, irrational, impulsive' maps onto it so cleanly.

The ego is partly conscious, runs on the reality principle and secondary process, and rationally delays gratification to fit the world; the superego is the internalized moral conscience and ego-ideal that judges right and wrong. A defence mechanism is a tactic the ego uses against anxiety, not a personality structure at all.
'Immediate gratification, irrational, impulsive, instinctual, pleasure' points at the id; 'realistic, planning, delay, mediating' at the ego; 'moral, ideal, conscience' at the superego.

wrong.b: Runs on the reality principle, mediating realistically among id, superego and the external world, the opposite of impulsive gratification. The central decision-maker, but its hallmark is delay and realism.
wrong.c: The moral conscience and ego-ideal that restrains the id and punishes transgressions with guilt. Moralistic and inhibiting, the antithesis of irrational immediate gratification.
wrong.d: Ego strategies (repression, projection, etc.) that manage anxiety: processes, not the impulsive drive structure. Unconscious like the id, but the question describes the instinctual seat of impulses.

q: According to Jung, the archetype representing the masculine side of females is called:
who: Carl Jung, Analytical Psychology

concept.t: In Carl Jung's analytical psychology the animus is the unconscious masculine archetype present within a woman.

Jung held that the collective unconscious, the inherited, species-wide stratum that was his decisive break from Sigmund Freud, contains universal archetypes. Among them is a contrasexual pair: each woman carries an inner masculine image, the animus, just as each man carries an inner feminine image, the anima.

It embodies a woman's unconscious masculine qualities (assertiveness, logic, the drive toward opinion, judgment and action) and colours how she relates to men, often via projection, and to her own initiative and authority. Becoming aware of and integrating it is part of individuation, unifying conscious and unconscious into a whole Self; left unexamined, it can show as rigid, dogmatic, argumentative opinionatedness.

The shadow is the repressed, instinctual dark side (loosely like Freud's id); the persona is the outward social mask. Placing Jung historically, he founded Analytical Psychology after his 1913 split from Freud, substituting a symbolic, spiritual, growth-oriented model for Freud's sexual-drive theory.
Animus is the masculine-within-the-female; anima is the feminine-within-the-male. The masculine side of a female is the animus: the exact mirror of the anima question, so keep the direction straight.

wrong.b: The repressed, instinctual dark side of the psyche, roughly like Sigmund Freud's id. A core Jungian archetype, but about disowned instinct and 'darkness', not gender.
wrong.c: The public mask worn to satisfy social demands and present an acceptable face. A famous Jungian term, but about the outward social self, not an inner gendered archetype.
wrong.d: The exact reverse archetype: the unconscious feminine image within a man. The strongest decoy, since the two differ only in direction; the masculine side of a female is the animus.

q: Alfred Adler proposed that humans are motivated by
who: Alfred Adler, Individual Psychology (1911)

concept.t: Alfred Adler broke from Sigmund Freud and argued that humans are motivated fundamentally by social, not sexual, forces.

An early member of Freud's Vienna circle, Adler left in 1911 to found Individual Psychology, rejecting Freud's grounding of motivation in libido and instinctual sexual and aggressive drives. He recast the person as an inherently social being whose strivings unfold within, and are oriented toward, a community.

His central motive is striving for superiority (or perfection/completion), the push from a felt inferiority toward competence and mastery, always in a social context. Crucially, healthy striving is governed by social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefuhl), an innate but cultivable sense of belonging and concern for others: the well-adjusted channel it into socially useful goals, the maladjusted chase personal superiority at others' expense.

Adler also stressed birth order, the unique goal-directed style of life and the creative self. Together these make him the forerunner of the more socially and culturally oriented neo-Freudians (Karen Horney, Erich Fromm, Harry Stack Sullivan) who followed.
Freud says sex and instinct drive us; Adler says social urges, belonging and striving for superiority within community. When the named motivator is Adler's, the answer is social urges.

wrong.a: Too vague; it does not name Adler's specific claim. Adler did stress more conscious, goal-directed striving than Sigmund Freud's deep unconscious, but his distinctive answer to what motivates us is the social dimension.
wrong.b: Karen Horney's concept: her ten compulsive interpersonal strategies condensed into the three neurotic trends. A fellow social-minded neo-Freudian, but this is her account of pathology, not Adler's theory of normal motivation.
wrong.c: A therapeutic stance from Carl Rogers' humanistic, person-centred approach, a different force of psychology. It concerns how a therapist relates to a client, not what drives human behaviour.

q: 'Many mental disorders can be traced to unconscious urges or impulses and to the struggle over their expression that takes place in the hidden depths of human personality'. The above statement is related to which one of the following perspectives?
who: Psychodynamic perspective, from Sigmund Freud and successors

concept.t: The statement locates mental disorder in unconscious urges and the inner struggle over expressing them, the signature claim of the psychodynamic perspective.

Growing from Sigmund Freud and his successors, it holds that much of mental life is unconscious and personality runs on perpetual conflict between instinctual drives (id), morality (superego) and reality (ego). Socially unacceptable wishes are pushed out of awareness by repression and other defence mechanisms, but the buried drives keep pressing for discharge.

Symptoms and disorders are compromise formations, the visible result of the hidden tug-of-war between forbidden impulses and the forces holding them down. 'Hidden depths of human personality' and 'struggle over their expression' are pure psychodynamic language.

Humanistic (Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow): blocked self-actualization and incongruence, stressing growth, choice and the present, not buried conflict. Social learning (Bandura): observation, modeling and reinforcement, not the dynamic unconscious or the past. Gestalt: perceptual organization, present awareness and the structuring of wholes; each rival downplays what this statement foregrounds.

Any statement tracing disorder to unconscious impulses and intrapsychic conflict over their expression is psychodynamic, the only one of the four that makes the buried, conflicted unconscious the cause of pathology.

wrong.a: Concerns perceptual organization and the apprehension of wholes ('the whole is other than the sum of its parts'); its therapy offshoot stresses present-moment awareness. It posits no unconscious drives causing disorder.
wrong.b: Attributes problems to blocked self-actualization, conditions of worth and incongruence between self and experience. It deliberately rejects the dark, conflict-ridden unconscious in favour of growth and choice.
wrong.c: Explains behaviour through observation, imitation, modeling and reinforcement, with no dynamic unconscious or repressed impulses. It locates causes in the observable environment and learning history, not 'the hidden depths of personality'.

q: The defence mechanism involving an intellectual reason to justify a certain action connected only in the mind of the person after the behaviour is completed is:
who: Named by Ernest Jones (1908); catalogued by Anna Freud (1936)

concept.t: Rationalisation is the only listed defence that supplies an after-the-fact intellectual justification: a reason the person builds in their own mind only once the behaviour is already complete.

A defence mechanism is an unconscious strategy the ego uses to reduce the anxiety that erupts when a forbidden id-impulse, or an ugly truth about oneself, threatens to reach awareness. It belongs to classical psychoanalysis, the first force of depth psychology, founded by Sigmund Freud in fin-de-siecle Vienna in the 1890s and 1900s.

Freud sketched the defences, but his daughter Anna Freud systematised them in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936), pivoting the movement from Freud's drive-focus toward the ego psychology school (later Heinz Hartmann). Rationalisation was named by Freud's English follower Ernest Jones in 1908; historically, later ego psychologists refined this defence family, sharpening the line between self-deceiving justification and honest reasoning.
