Around 1968, Maslow was among those who announced a fourth force for experiences the first three could not capture: spirituality, transcendence, mystical states and peak experiences beyond the individual ego. 'Trans-personal' means 'beyond the personal': the self can extend past ordinary identity into a wider, sometimes spiritual, awareness, like the unity reported in deep meditation.

Maslow helped found both; the fourth force grew out of the third when humanists found self-actualization sometimes opened onto transcendent experiences their framework could not explain. Yet the two are counted as separate forces.
Transpersonal psychology is the fourth force, distinct from psychoanalysis, behaviourism and humanism, and defined by transcendence and spiritual experience.

wrong.a: Not one of the named forces. The word echoes humanistic and Gestalt language about lived, present experience, but no historically numbered 'force' carries this name.
wrong.b: The second force (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), not the fourth. It studies observable, conditioned behaviour and explicitly rejects the inner and spiritual phenomena of the transpersonal fourth force, so it is doubly wrong.
wrong.d: The first force (Sigmund Freud), not the fourth. It does explore hidden, non-conscious mind, but that is the personal unconscious, not transcendence beyond the ego.

q: Maslow considers physiological and safety needs truly as
who: Abraham Maslow, hierarchy of needs (1943)

concept.t: In Maslow's framework, physiological and safety needs sit at the very base of the pyramid: the basic, lower tier.

In Systems & Theories, Abraham Maslow, a founder of humanistic psychology (the third force, with Carl Rogers), offered a humanistic alternative to behaviourist drive-reduction and Freudian instinct theory. His 1943 paper A Theory of Human Motivation arranged human motives in an ascending hierarchy.

Picture a five-level pyramid: at the bottom physiological needs (food, water, sleep, warmth), then safety needs (security, shelter, stability). The lower four levels (physiological, safety, social, esteem) are deficiency needs (D-needs): they arise from deprivation and create tension until satisfied. The top level, self-actualization, is a growth need (B-need, for Being), driven by the desire to develop rather than fill a lack.

Under prepotency, lower needs must be reasonably met before higher ones motivate, which is exactly why these are called lower: a starving person is preoccupied with food long before reputation or growth. Calling them 'lower' is about position, not importance; they are in fact the most urgent.
Physiological and safety needs are the lower, basic deficiency needs at the foundation of Maslow's hierarchy.

wrong.a: In Maslow's model these are esteem and especially self-actualization, at the top of the pyramid. Physiological and safety needs sit at the base: the lower, prepotent needs that must be met before higher ones activate.
wrong.c: Not a Maslow term. A clever trap, since physiological needs ARE the most prepotent (most urgent and dominant when unmet), but Maslow's actual classification is 'lower' (basic) needs.
wrong.d: Not part of Maslow's hierarchy at all: a fabricated-sounding label that may appeal because self-actualization involves personal transformation. No level carries this name, least of all the base.

q: Which ONE of the following is not a major construct of existential theory?
who: Freudian psychoanalysis, not existential theory (May, Frankl, Yalom)

concept.t: Uncovering unconscious fears and desires is a psychoanalytic aim, not an existential one, so it is the construct that does not belong.

In Systems & Theories, existential psychology is a close cousin of humanism; both belong to the broad 'third force' reaction against Sigmund Freud and behaviourism. Where Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers stressed positive growth, existential thinkers like Rollo May, Viktor Frankl and later Irvin Yalom focused on the harder 'givens' of existence, drawing on philosophers such as Kierkegaard, Heidegger and Sartre.

Irvin Yalom names four ultimate concerns: death (confronting our mortality), freedom (and the responsibility it imposes), isolation (being ultimately alone) and meaninglessness. Therapy centres on coming to terms with the anxiety these produce, so a person lives authentically rather than fleeing into avoidance; death, isolation and anxiety, three of the options, map directly onto these.

Excavating buried, unconscious fears and desires is the project of Freudian psychoanalysis (the first force), which assumes hidden material from early life drives present behaviour and that cure comes from making the unconscious conscious. Existential therapy works with conscious, present awareness of existence: it asks how you will live with given truths, not what repressed wish lurks beneath.
Existential theory deals with death, freedom, isolation and meaning; uncovering the unconscious belongs to psychoanalysis.

wrong.a: True: often called existential angst, anxiety is the natural response to confronting freedom, death and isolation. Anxiety also features in psychoanalysis and other therapies, but here it is squarely existential.
wrong.b: True: one of Irvin Yalom's four ultimate existential concerns, arguably the defining one. It may seem morbid, but death awareness is the heart of existential theory.
wrong.d: True: another of Yalom's existential givens. However connected we are, each person ultimately faces existence alone; bleak, but a core existential concern.

q: ______ is associated with the Gestalt school of psychology.
who: Max Wertheimer, with Koffka and Kohler, phi phenomenon (1912)

concept.t: Max Wertheimer is the founder most directly associated with the Gestalt school of psychology.

In Systems & Theories, Gestalt psychology arose in early-twentieth-century Germany against structuralism (Wilhelm Wundt, Edward Titchener), which broke consciousness into elementary sensations, and against the atomism of associationism. The German word Gestalt means 'form', 'shape' or 'whole': perception organises sensory elements into wholes that are more than the sum of their parts ('the whole is other than the sum of its parts').

Wertheimer launched the movement in 1912 with the phi phenomenon, the illusion of apparent motion when two stationary lights flash in sequence (the basis of cinema and neon signs). It proved the mind actively constructs experience rather than passively recording isolated sensations, directly refuting the structuralist program.

His collaborators Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Kohler (famous for insight learning in chimpanzees) made up the three founders; their work later influenced cognitive psychology and, through Fritz Perls, Gestalt therapy. Seeing a melody as a unified tune rather than separate notes is a classic Gestalt illustration.

Max Wertheimer, with Koffka and Kohler, founded Gestalt psychology: phi phenomenon and whole-over-parts. Contrast John Watson (behaviourism), William James (American functionalism) and Ivan Pavlov (classical conditioning).

wrong.a: Founded behaviourism in 1913 ('Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It'), studying only observable stimulus-response behaviour. It emerged almost alongside Gestalt but is the opposite: it rejects the study of perception and inner organisation.
wrong.b: Led American functionalism and wrote The Principles of Psychology, studying how mental processes help organisms adapt. Functionalism concerns the purpose of mind, not the German Gestalt focus on perceptual wholes.
wrong.c: Known for classical conditioning and reflexology (the salivating-dog experiments). His behavioural/physiological tradition of learned reflexes is the antithesis of Gestalt's holistic perception.

q: Humanistic and Phenomenological approaches have been criticised for:
who: Sociological and cross-cultural critics of humanism

concept.t: Humanistic and phenomenological approaches concentrate so heavily on the individual's inner world that they can overlook the social and cultural forces that shape it.

In Systems & Theories, the phenomenological method, inherited from philosophers like Husserl and central to humanistic psychology (the third force), studies experience from the person's own first-person point of view, treating subjective perception as the proper object of study. Carl Rogers built person-centred therapy around the self-concept and personal frame of reference; Abraham Maslow traced motivation to needs within the person.

This inward focus was a deliberate corrective to behaviourism's neglect of inner life and psychoanalysis's deterministic drives, and is the school's defining strength. It is also the root of the standard criticism from sociological and cross-cultural critics: privileging the self neglects the social, cultural, economic and political structures that shape how identity forms.

Someone raised in poverty, under caste oppression or within a particular cultural script is moulded by forces the purely individual lens can miss; even self-actualization may reflect Western, individualistic assumptions. Critics also note that heavy reliance on subjective experience makes the approach hard to test with rigorous scientific methods.
The recognised weakness of humanistic and phenomenological psychology is neglect of wider social and cultural context, precisely because they centre the individual's inner experience.

wrong.a: The self-concept does involve perception, but these approaches stress holistic, felt, subjective experience, not information-processing cognition (the cognitive school's territory), so this is not the criticism they attract.
wrong.c: The exact opposite of the truth, set to catch careless reading: phenomenological and humanistic psychology are precisely the schools that prioritise personal experience and subjective perception.
wrong.d: That criticism fits the psychodynamic approach, which roots present behaviour in early childhood. Humanism stresses the present, future potential and the actualizing tendency, so this misassigns a psychoanalytic weakness.

q: In order from lowest to highest, what are Maslow's classes of needs?
who: Abraham Maslow, hierarchy of needs (1943)

concept.t: It is the exact lowest-to-highest order of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs; only this option preserves the genuine ascent without swapping any level.

In Systems & Theories, Maslow, a founder of humanistic psychology (the third force) with Carl Rogers, proposed in his 1943 paper A Theory of Human Motivation that motivation is arranged in tiers people climb from the bottom up, a humanistic alternative to behaviourist and Freudian accounts.

Build it level by level: physiological (food, water, sleep, warmth), safety (security, stability), social (love, belonging, acceptance; also called belongingness needs), esteem (respect, achievement, self-worth), and at the summit self-actualization (realising one's full potential). The first four are deficiency needs arising from a lack; the top is a growth need driven by the desire to develop.

Under prepotency, a lower-level deficit need must be reasonably satisfied before the next level becomes a strong motivator: someone struggling for safety is not driven mainly by esteem, and someone fighting for basic survival rarely pursues growth projects first. Knowing the order cold is the whole test here.
The ascending sequence is physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualization: deficiency needs below, the single growth need on top.

wrong.a: Scrambles the base, placing physiological and safety ABOVE social instead of at the foundation. In Maslow's prepotency rule, survival needs always come first.
wrong.b: A near-miss that swaps the top two: esteem (the fourth level) must precede self-actualization (the fifth and highest), so reversing them breaks the hierarchy.
wrong.d: The whole hierarchy inverted, highest need first, catching anyone who misreads 'lowest to highest' as 'highest to lowest'. Reading direction matters: self-actualization is the top, not the start.

q: Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers were the proponents of ______ approach
who: Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers, humanistic third force (1950s)

concept.t: Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers are the two defining proponents of the humanistic approach.

In Systems & Theories, by the mid-twentieth century psychoanalysis (the first force) and behaviourism (the second force) dominated, both seen as deterministic and pessimistic. Maslow and Rogers founded humanistic psychology in the 1950s as the third force, an explicit alternative restoring the whole person, free will and the positive potential of human nature to the centre of the field.

The hierarchy of needs, a model of motivation culminating in self-actualization, the realisation of one's full potential; he also described the qualities of self-actualized people and their peak experiences.

Person-centred (client-centred) therapy and the theories of the self-concept, the ideal self, the actualizing tendency and unconditional positive regard, the warm, non-judgmental acceptance that lets a person grow. Both stress the whole individual over isolated behaviours or symptoms, conscious experience, free will and a growth-oriented view of human nature; treating clients as capable of self-direction, not objects to be shaped, is a concrete marker of humanism.

Maslow and Rogers are the proponents of the humanistic approach, the third force focused on the whole person and self-actualization. Contrast cognitive (information processing), behavioural (conditioning and reinforcement) and existential (a near relative: meaning, freedom, confronting death).

wrong.a: Studies mental processes such as memory, attention, perception and thinking, linked to figures like Ulric Neisser and George Miller. Its subject is information processing, not the whole-person growth model Maslow and Rogers built.
wrong.b: John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner: observable conditioning and reinforcement, rejecting the study of inner experience. It is the very second force humanism reacted against, the opposite of Maslow and Rogers's emphasis on inner experience and free will.
wrong.d: Rollo May and Viktor Frankl: the closest distractor, sharing the third-force, whole-person spirit. But its specific focus is meaning, freedom, responsibility and death; Maslow and Rogers are specifically the humanists.

q: The striving for fulfilment of one's potential is called
who: Abraham Maslow, self-actualization (top of the hierarchy of needs)

concept.t: Self-actualization is precisely the term for striving to fulfil one's full potential.

In Systems & Theories, it is the centerpiece of humanistic psychology (the third force, founded by Abraham Maslow and Rogers as an answer to behaviourism and psychoanalysis) and sits at the very top of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs as the highest growth need.

Maslow defined it as the drive to become everything one is capable of becoming, realising one's talents, creativity and deepest capacities once the lower deficiency needs are reasonably met. A self-actualized individual is autonomous, accepting of self and others, problem-centred and prone to peak experiences of profound fulfilment.

Carl Rogers' fully functioning person lives openly and authentically in line with their true self, propelled by the actualizing tendency. Distinguish self-concept (one's overall self-image), self-efficacy (a Bandura term from social-cognitive theory: belief in succeeding at specific tasks) and the ideal self (Rogers: the person one wishes to be); only self-actualization names the active striving toward full potential itself.
Realising one's full potential is self-actualization, the peak of Maslow's hierarchy.

wrong.a: The overall organised set of beliefs and perceptions one holds about oneself (a key Rogers construct). A humanistic 'self' term, but a static self-image, not the active striving to fulfil potential.
wrong.b: Albert Bandura's social-cognitive term: belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task or situation. It sounds achievement-oriented, but it is task-specific confidence, not the broad drive to realise one's whole potential.
wrong.d: Rogers' term for the version of oneself a person wishes to be, contrasted with the actual self-concept; a large gap causes incongruence. It is a goal image, not the actualizing striving itself.

q: The concept of 'Here-and-Now' is popular in
who: Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler); Fritz Perls' Gestalt therapy

concept.t: The official key ties the here-and-now emphasis to the holistic Gestalt perspective.

In Systems & Theories, Gestalt psychology was founded by Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Kohler in early-twentieth-century Germany, reacting against structuralism's element-by-element analysis. Experience must be grasped as an organised whole, since the meaning of any element depends on the total configuration it sits within.

The here-and-now is a focus on present, immediate awareness of experience as it unfolds, not the distant past or the abstract future; it flows from the principle that perception and experience are organised wholes apprehended in the present moment. Fritz Perls carried it into Gestalt therapy, bringing clients back to what they feel and notice right now, in this room, as the route to awareness and integration.

The present-moment focus is also strongly valued in humanistic-existential therapy, so more than one perspective has a genuine claim; the key assigns it specifically to the holistic Gestalt view, and that is the answer to reproduce. In contrast, behaviourism (external stimulus-response links) and cognitive psychology (internal information processing) do not centre present subjective awareness.
A therapist asking 'what are you aware of right now?' rather than probing childhood is the concrete Gestalt move: the here-and-now is keyed to Gestalt psychology's holistic perspective.

wrong.b: John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner: observable stimulus-response learning and reinforcement history, deliberately excluding subjective inner states. Present-moment awareness is exactly the inner experience behaviourism refuses to study.
wrong.c: Studies internal information processing: attention, memory and mental operations. It concerns the mind, but its object is the mechanics of cognition, not the felt, experiential here-and-now of immediate awareness.
wrong.d: Genuinely values present, lived experience: the strongest distractor and a defensible alternative. But the key assigns the here-and-now to the wholistic Gestalt perspective, so for this question it is the near-miss.

q: Which perspective is known as the "third force" in Psychology?
who: Maslow and Rogers (with Rollo May), humanistic third force (1950s)

concept.t: Humanistic psychology is the perspective universally called the third force.

In Systems & Theories, by the mid-twentieth century two schools dominated: psychoanalysis (first force, Sigmund Freud), explaining people through unconscious conflict and early experience, and behaviourism (second force, John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner), reducing behaviour to conditioning and reinforcement and largely ignoring inner life. Many found both too deterministic and pessimistic: Freudians saw people driven by buried drives, behaviourists by environmental contingencies.

In response, Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers (joined by Rollo May) founded humanistic psychology in the 1950s. It studies the whole person and the uniqueness of each individual, stressing free will, conscious experience and an innate drive toward self-actualization and growth; where the first two forces emphasised what constrains us, humanism emphasised what we can choose and become, restoring optimism and agency.

Later, a fourth force, transpersonal psychology, extended this toward transcendence, and cognitive psychology rose as a separate movement; neither is the third force. Humanism's optimistic, growth-centred view of human nature is its defining marker.
Humanism is the third force, an alternative to psychoanalysis and behaviourism that centres the whole, freely choosing person.

wrong.a: Freud's first force: unconscious conflict, repression and early childhood. It sits first in the numbered sequence and embodies the very determinism humanism reacted against.
wrong.b: The second force (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner): observable stimulus-response learning and reinforcement. It is numbered second and represents the environmental determinism humanism rejected.
wrong.c: Emerged later (the 'cognitive revolution' of the 1950s-60s), sometimes informally treated as a separate movement. It studies mental information processing, not growth, free will and potential, and never held the 'third force' title.

q: Which is NOT Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
who: Ego is Sigmund Freud's; the needs are Abraham Maslow's (1943)

concept.t: The ego is not a level in Maslow's hierarchy at all; it belongs to a completely different system. This Systems & Theories item deliberately mixes two frameworks.

Proposed by Abraham Maslow in 1943 within humanistic psychology (the third force), it is a theory of motivation. It runs from physiological needs (food, water, sleep) to safety (security, stability), belongingness and love (social connection), esteem (respect and achievement) and finally self-actualization (realising one's potential). Three options, physiological, safety and esteem, are authentic rungs of this ladder.

The ego comes from Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic model of personality structure (the first force): the id (primitive, instinctual, pleasure-seeking drives), the ego (the reality-oriented mediator balancing the id, superego and external world) and the superego (the internalised moral conscience). The ego manages conflict and operates on the reality principle; it is not a need to be satisfied and has nothing to do with a motivation hierarchy.

Confusing a humanistic motivation level with a psychoanalytic personality structure is the classic trap. Physiological, safety and esteem are Maslow's needs; the ego is a Freudian personality structure that does not belong in the hierarchy.

wrong.b: True: physiological needs (food, water, sleep, warmth) are the base, first level of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, so they are clearly in it.
wrong.c: True: safety needs (security, stability, shelter) are the second level of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, just above physiological needs; an authentic rung included to tempt a careless reader.
wrong.d: True: esteem needs (respect, achievement, recognition, self-worth) are the fourth level of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy, just below self-actualization. Esteem belongs to the hierarchy; the Freudian ego does not.

q: According to Maslow's Need of Hierarchy theory, which is the right sequence from lowest to highest order needs?
who: Abraham Maslow, A Theory of Human Motivation (1943)

concept.t: It keeps the genuine lowest-to-highest climb of Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs: physiological first, safety second, belongingness third. Only one option keeps that exact sequence; the rest shuffle it.

In Systems & Theories, Maslow was a founder of humanistic psychology (the third force) with Carl Rogers. His 1943 paper A Theory of Human Motivation arranged human motives in ascending tiers, a humanistic model of motivation set against behaviourist and psychoanalytic accounts.

Physiological needs (food, water, sleep, warmth) at the base, then safety needs (security and stability), belongingness and love needs (friendship, intimacy, acceptance), esteem needs (respect and achievement) and self-actualization at the summit. The first four are deficiency needs driven by lack; the peak is a growth need.

The ordering is governed by prepotency: a more basic need must be reasonably met before the next becomes a strong motivator, so a person fighting for physical survival is not yet driven mainly by the wish to belong. The question asks only about the first three rungs, but the same rule applies.
The correct ascending order begins physiological, then safety, then belongingness: in Maslow's principle, lower needs come first.

wrong.a: Swaps safety and belongingness, placing a social need before security. Security needs are more basic than the need to belong: Abraham Maslow's prepotency rule puts safety second and belongingness third.
wrong.c: Puts safety before physiological needs. Both feel 'basic', but physiological needs (food, water, sleep) are the absolute foundation, so starting with safety inverts the base of the hierarchy.
wrong.d: The most scrambled option, tempting only on a careless read: belongingness is the third-level social need, not the lowest, so starting with it contradicts Abraham Maslow's ascending order.

q: Which among the following suggests that all individuals possess an innate tendency to grow and develop?
who: Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers, humanistic third force (1950s)

concept.t: The Humanistic perspective is built squarely on the belief that everyone has an innate tendency to grow and develop. Only humanism makes this growth assumption its centrepiece, so 'all of the above' fails.

In Systems & Theories, humanism is the third force, founded by Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers in the 1950s as a deliberate reaction against the pessimism of psychoanalysis (first force) and the determinism of behaviourism (second force). Where Sigmund Freud saw people driven by conflicted unconscious instincts, and John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner saw them shaped passively by conditioning, humanism treats human nature as fundamentally positive and forward-moving.

Rogers called the built-in drive the actualizing tendency: the organism's natural push to maintain, enhance and develop its full capacities, much as a plant grows toward light given warmth, water and soil. For a person the 'right conditions' include unconditional positive regard. Maslow expressed the same optimism through self-actualization at the top of his hierarchy, the realisation of one's full potential.

It looks at the whole individual and stresses free will, self-efficacy and conscious striving. A concrete marker: the therapist's faith that, given the right conditions, a client will naturally move toward health.
The innate tendency to grow and self-actualize is the defining assumption of the humanistic perspective.

wrong.a: In contrast, Sigmund Freud and successors stress unconscious conflict, instinctual drives and early childhood determinism: a person shaped by buried forces, a conflicted picture of human nature, not a benign innate drive to grow.
wrong.c: Studies information processing, perception, memory and thinking, treating the mind like a computational system. It concerns inner mental life but makes no claim about an inborn tendency toward growth and self-development.
wrong.d: Only humanism centres on the innate growth (actualizing) tendency; the psychodynamic and cognitive perspectives do not, so the inclusive option fails.

q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a 'figure'?
who: Gestalt figure-ground: Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler

concept.t: Diffused and spatially distant describes the ground, not the figure. Smaller, clearly outlined and higher in object character all belong to the figure.

In Systems & Theories, figure-ground organisation is a foundational principle of Gestalt psychology, founded by Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka and Wolfgang Kohler. It shows the mind actively organises sensory input into structured wholes rather than passively registering isolated sensations.

When we perceive a scene, the mind splits it into a figure, the object of focus that stands out with a definite shape, and the ground, the background it is seen against. The figure is distinct and well-contoured with clear outlines, tends to appear smaller, closer to the observer and higher in 'object character' (it looks like a definite thing). The ground seems shapeless, less defined, spatially distant and recedes behind the figure, with the contour 'belonging' to the figure.
The Rubin vase flips between a vase (figure) on a dark ground and two faces (figure) on a light ground, but never both at once, showing the organisation is something the mind imposes.
The figure is distinct, outlined, smaller and closer; diffused and distant describes the ground.

wrong.a: True of the figure: it is typically seen as a compact, bounded object standing out against a larger surrounding ground. Listed to tempt a reader who reverses the rule.
wrong.b: True of the figure: well-defined contours. The contour or boundary is perceived as belonging to the figure, giving it a definite edge while the ground stays shapeless.
wrong.c: True of the figure, not the ground: the thing-like quality of looking like a definite object. It tempts only if you confuse the two regions.

q: Which of the following is not associated with the humanistic perspective of psychopathology?
who: Reinforcement: B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning, not humanism

concept.t: Reinforcement is a behaviourist concept and has no place in the humanistic view of psychopathology.

In Systems & Theories, the humanistic perspective is the third force, founded by Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers as an alternative to psychoanalysis (first force) and behaviourism (second force). On this view, distress arises when natural growth toward self-actualization is blocked, often because the person received only conditional acceptance and developed incongruence between real self and self-concept.

Its therapeutic hallmarks are a deep belief in human potential, unconditional positive regard (warm, non-judgmental acceptance of the person regardless of behaviour) and a respectful, genuine therapist attitude including empathy and congruence, the 'core conditions' Rogers identified. Together these create a safe space in which the client's own actualizing tendency can resume.

Reinforcement comes from B.F. Skinner and operant conditioning in behaviourism: strengthening responses through rewards or consequences, shaping the person from outside rather than growth from within. Importing it into the humanistic frame mixes two opposed views of human nature: an active, self-directing organism versus a product of environmental contingencies.
Human potential, unconditional positive regard and a respectful stance are humanistic; reinforcement is a behaviourist idea. That clash is exactly what the question tests.

wrong.a: True: a core humanistic assumption, the conviction that people have an innate capacity to grow toward self-actualization given the right conditions.
wrong.b: True: Carl Rogers' unconditional positive regard, the warm, non-judgmental acceptance central to person-centred humanistic therapy that lets the client's actualizing tendency resume.
wrong.d: True: the Rogerian core conditions of empathy and congruence (a respectful, genuine attitude), the hallmark of person-centred humanistic practice. Included to tempt a careless reader.

q: Which of the following should not be exhibited by a true sportsman?
who: Sportsmanship in sport psychology (positive-psychology strengths)

concept.t: A win-at-all-costs attitude contradicts the very ideals of sportsmanship.

In Systems & Theories, this sits in the humanistic/positive-psychology stream applied to sport psychology, which studies psychological factors in athletic performance and well-being and values healthy character, not just outcomes. Sportsmanship is the ethical and emotional disposition to play fairly, treat opponents and officials with respect, and value the integrity of the contest above the result.

Persistence (keeping going through setbacks; grit and resilience), self-control (regulating emotion, staying calm under pressure; emotional self-regulation) and optimism (a positive explanatory style that supports recovery from failure; Martin Seligman's learned optimism). All three serve performance and well-being and reflect positive psychology's strengths-based view of the person.

It prizes the outcome so highly that it erodes fairness and composure, encouraging cheating, aggression and loss of emotional control when things go wrong. It treats victory as the only value, the opposite of fair play and good character, and is linked to poorer long-term well-being. A true sportsman congratulates a stronger opponent rather than disputing every call.
Persistence, self-control and optimism mark a true sportsman; focusing on winning at all costs is the trait to reject.

wrong.a: A positive, adaptive trait (akin to grit and resilience): the determination to keep going through setbacks. A true sportsman SHOULD show it.
wrong.b: Regulating one's emotions and staying composed under pressure, especially after bad calls or losses, is a hallmark of sportsmanship, not something a true sportsman should avoid.
wrong.c: A positive outlook supporting resilience and recovery from failure, in line with Martin Seligman's learned optimism: a desirable quality a true sportsman SHOULD show.

q: Which perspective is often referred to as the 'third force' in Psychology?
who: Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers, humanistic psychology (1950s)

concept.t: In Systems & Theories, humanistic psychology is the perspective known as the third force.

In the early and mid-twentieth century two schools held sway: psychoanalysis (first force, Sigmund Freud), explaining people through unconscious drives and early conflict, and behaviourism (second force, John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner), explaining behaviour through conditioning and reinforcement while ignoring inner experience. Both were seen as deterministic, casting people as driven by forces they could not control.

Reacting against this, Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers founded humanistic psychology in the 1950s, joined by figures such as Rollo May. It studies the whole person and the uniqueness of each individual, emphasising free will, conscious choice, subjective experience and the innate drive toward self-actualization.

Where the earlier forces stressed constraint, humanism stressed potential and personal responsibility, restoring optimism and agency to psychology's view of human nature. Its concrete markers: an optimistic, growth-oriented view of human nature and respect for subjective experience.
Distinguish the distractors by their systems: humanism is the third force, the whole-person alternative to psychoanalysis and behaviourism.

wrong.a: George Engel's integrative model of health and illness across biological, psychological and social levels. Respected and modern, but a model of health, not one of psychology's three historically numbered forces.
wrong.b: The second force (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner): observable stimulus-response learning, and the deterministic approach humanism reacted against. Numbered second, not third.
wrong.c: Studies mental information processing and is sometimes loosely called a later wave or movement, but it never carried the historically conferred 'third force' label, which belongs to humanism.

q: "Each person must continually recreate himself, The meaning of life and of existence is never fixed; rather, it constantly changes." This can be best explained by-
who: Rollo May, Viktor Frankl; Sartre's 'existence precedes essence'

concept.t: The idea that meaning is never fixed and each person must continually recreate themselves is the heart of existential thought.

In Systems & Theories, existential psychology is part of the broad third-force movement (alongside humanism) that rejected the determinism of psychoanalysis and behaviourism. Its content comes from existential philosophy (Soren Kierkegaard, Martin Heidegger, Jean-Paul Sartre), brought into psychology by Rollo May and Viktor Frankl, and later Irvin Yalom.

There is no pre-given essence or fixed purpose handed to us; existence comes first and we define ourselves through the choices we make. Sartre's formula 'existence precedes essence' captures this: a person is not a finished thing but an ongoing project, perpetually authoring their own meaning.

With freedom come responsibility and the anxiety of choosing without guarantees; the task is to live authentically in the face of death and uncertainty. Existential therapists look past mere symptom reduction to how a client defines meaning, purpose and a life well lived (Frankl's logotherapy is one example).

Distinguish the close option: humanism centres on self-actualization and the positive actualizing tendency. Meaning that is never fixed and must be continually recreated through free choice is existential psychology.

wrong.a: The strongest distractor: also third-force, choice- and growth-affirming. But humanism centres on self-actualization and an innate positive growth tendency; radical, ever-shifting self-creation is the specifically existential emphasis.
wrong.c: A methodological tradition studying behaviour and mental processes through controlled scientific experiments: an approach to method, not a philosophy of meaning or existence.
wrong.d: The broader parent discipline from which existentialism springs, and the quote sounds philosophical. But the question asks for the best PSYCHOLOGICAL framing, which is existential psychology.

q: Which psychologist's work on Basic Anxiety aligns closely with Karen Horney's conception of neurosis and feelings of helplessness in the Indian context?
who: Sudhir Kakar, India's cultural psychoanalyst, after Karen Horney

concept.t: Sudhir Kakar applies psychoanalytic ideas like basic anxiety to the Indian context, aligning most closely with Karen Horney's conception of neurosis and helplessness.

In Systems & Theories, Horney was a neo-Freudian who revised classical psychoanalysis by stressing social and cultural factors over Sigmund Freud's biological drives. She argued neurosis grows out of basic anxiety, a deep feeling of helplessness and insecurity a child develops in a threatening or unloving environment, leading to defensive interpersonal strategies (moving toward, against or away from people).

India's foremost cultural psychoanalyst, he took Western psychoanalytic concepts and reinterpreted them through Indian childhood, family structure, religion and culture. He examined how patterns of dependence, the joint family and early mother-child relationships shape the Indian individual's inner world, bridging psychoanalysis with indigenous experience in the same socially-grounded spirit as Horney.

Distinguish the other Indian names: major figures, but none maps onto Horney's basic anxiety. Sudhir Kakar, India's cultural psychoanalyst, connects Horney's basic anxiety and helplessness to the Indian context.

wrong.a: Known for self and identity in Indian psychological thought, integrating Indian philosophical traditions with Western psychology: an indigenous philosophical angle, not Karen Horney's psychoanalytic basic anxiety.
wrong.b: Adapted projective techniques such as the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) for the Indian context: projective assessment, not linking Karen Horney's basic anxiety and neurosis to Indian culture.
wrong.d: A foundational figure in Indian social and cross-cultural psychology, known for work on deprivation and the indigenization of psychology. Perhaps the best-known name listed, but not Horneyan psychoanalysis of basic anxiety.

q: ____ is a source of knowledge as per Empiricists.
who: Empiricism: John Locke's tabula rasa; David Hume, George Berkeley

concept.t: Empiricism, by definition, roots every piece of knowledge in what the senses deliver.

Epistemology is the branch of philosophy that asks where knowledge comes from and how we justify it. Empiricism answers that the mind begins essentially empty and is filled only by what we see, hear, touch, taste and smell. It privileges observation, empirical evidence and substantiation over truths supposedly built into the mind.

John Locke pictured the mind as a tabula rasa, a blank slate written on by lived experience; David Hume and George Berkeley argued even abstract ideas are faded copies or recombinations of earlier sensory impressions. The great rival, rationalism (René Descartes, Leibniz, Spinoza), credits reason and innate ideas; a third stance, skepticism, doubts certainty altogether.

In Systems & Theories of psychology, empiricism is a deep taproot: when psychology broke from philosophy in 1879 under Wilhelm Wundt, it inherited the demand that mind be studied through observable data, not armchair speculation. It later hardened into behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner), which counted only observable, sensory-measurable behaviour as science, and the British associationists who built mental life from sensations were direct descendants. The cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s (Ulric Neisser, Miller) softened pure empiricism by readmitting internal representations, yet still grounded theory in measurable evidence.

Empiricism says knowledge comes from sensory experience; rationalism credits reason and innate ideas. It is no relic but the methodological backbone running from Locke through Wundt and behaviourism into modern experimental psychology.

wrong.a: The signature claim of rationalism (René Descartes, Leibniz), empiricism's direct opposite. For empiricists, reasoning only rearranges material the senses first supplied; reason alone is not their source.
wrong.b: Constructed, abstract explanations, not the raw input empiricists treat as the origin of knowledge. A theory must itself be built from and tested against observation: a product of the empiricist process, never its source.
wrong.d: Pure introspective or meditative thought within the mind; as a self-sufficient source of truth it belongs to rationalist and innate-idea traditions. Empiricism denies that inward reflection unaided by the senses can originate knowledge.

q: The point at which a stimulus becomes strong enough to trigger a response only 50% of the time is
who: Gustav Fechner's psychophysics: the 50 percent absolute threshold

concept.t: A threshold is, by definition, the stimulus level at which a response is triggered on half of all attempts.

Psychophysics, founded by Gustav Fechner, quantifies the lawful relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce. Senses do not switch on at a single fixed value: near the limit, fluctuations in attention, fatigue and background neural noise make detection probabilistic rather than all-or-none, so researchers use a statistical cutoff. The absolute threshold is the minimum intensity detected on 50 percent of trials; the difference threshold or just noticeable difference (JND) is the smallest detectable change, noticed half the time.

In Systems & Theories, psychophysics, born in the 1850s-60s with Weber and Fechner, was the very first rigorously quantitative psychology. It gave Wundt the experimental respectability to open his Leipzig laboratory in 1879, proving mind could be measured and paving the way for structuralism.

Crucially, the threshold survived the long behaviourist eclipse and re-emerged as a cornerstone of the cognitive revolution, where the information-processing model treats the observer as a limited-capacity system whose detection is probabilistic. Signal detection theory later refined the idea by separating true sensitivity from decision bias. So the threshold links classical psychophysics to the mind as an information channel coping with noise.
A threshold is the cutoff intensity at which a stimulus first triggers a response on at least 50 percent of occasions tested.

wrong.b: A signal detection theory concept: an observer's standing tendency to answer 'yes' or 'no' regardless of the stimulus. A decision criterion (how willing someone is to report a signal), never the 50 percent intensity.
wrong.c: Signal detection theory (SDT; Green and Swets) is a framework separating true sensitivity from decision bias. It grew from threshold research but challenges the classical threshold idea rather than naming the 50 percent point.
wrong.d: The Gestalt illusion of apparent motion when stationary lights flash in sequence, demonstrated by Max Wertheimer. It concerns perceived movement, not detection limits or the 50 percent cutoff.

q: Every Just Noticeable Difference in stimulation constitutes a constant increment in sensation magnitude. Who among the following had given this assumption?
who: Gustav Fechner, Elements of Psychophysics (1860)

concept.t: Fechner supplied the assumption that every just noticeable difference adds one equal step of sensation.

Ernst Weber discovered that the just noticeable difference (JND) is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed absolute amount: a candle is obvious in a dark room but lost in daylight.

Gustav Fechner, founder of psychophysics, assumed each JND, wherever it falls on the scale, is one equal increment of subjective sensation. Treating every JND as a constant unit of felt experience, he integrated across these steps and derived that sensation grows in proportion to the logarithm of physical intensity, the Weber-Fechner law. This is why doubling a light's energy yields only a modest rise in perceived brightness.

In Systems & Theories, Fechner's 1860 Elements of Psychophysics was arguably the first truly quantitative law in psychology, the hinge on which it became a science. By showing the mental could be mathematically related to the physical, it gave Wundt the tools and credibility to launch experimental psychology in 1879, seeding structuralism's attempt to measure conscious elements. The logarithmic scaling was later challenged by S. S. Stevens' power law, and the idea of a limited, noise-bound sensory system fed the information-processing thinking of the cognitive revolution.
Weber described the constant proportion of the JND; Fechner assumed each JND equals a constant increment of sensation.

wrong.a: Pioneered the experimental study of memory with nonsense syllables (forgetting curve, savings method). Another nineteenth-century quantitative pioneer often listed beside Weber and Fechner, but his domain was memory and learning, not sensation magnitude.
wrong.b: Discovered the empirical regularity, Weber's law: the JND is a constant fraction of the stimulus. His name is half of 'Weber-Fechner', but Fechner added the equal-sensation-increment assumption.
wrong.c: A neo-behaviourist known for cognitive maps, latent learning and purposive behaviourism in rats. His work on learning and intervening variables is decades and disciplines away from psychophysical scaling; no connection to JNDs.

q: One feature of the streaming of consciousness that received substantial attention by researchers is:
who: Teasdale and colleagues (1991); William James's stream of consciousness (1890)

concept.t: Daydreaming is the feature of the stream of consciousness that researchers examined most intensively.

William James, in his 1890 Principles of Psychology, coined the phrase stream of consciousness for thought that flows continuously and ever-changing rather than in discrete, separable chunks. Within that stream, attention does not stay on the external world; it drifts inward to images, memories and fantasies unrelated to the immediate surroundings.

This inward drift is daydreaming, also called stimulus-independent thought because its content is internally generated, not cued by the environment; it is the close ancestor of today's research on mind-wandering. Teasdale and colleagues (1991) studied how often such thoughts arise, what conditions provoke them, and how they relate to mood and concentration, making daydreaming the most carefully measured component of ongoing consciousness.

In Systems & Theories, consciousness was the founding subject of psychology under James's functionalism and Wundt-Titchener structuralism, but behaviourism banished it for half a century as unobservable and so unscientific. The cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s (Ulric Neisser, Miller) made internal mental events respectable again, treating the mind as an information processor whose attention can be directed outward or inward. Daydreaming research took James's century-old phenomenological insight and made it experimentally tractable.
Daydreaming is stimulus-independent, internally generated thought, the drifting feature of James's stream of consciousness that drew the most research.

wrong.a: A demographic individual-difference variable: something you could study about consciousness, not a structural feature of it. James's concept describes the flowing nature and contents of awareness in everyone.
wrong.c: Physiological correlates of mental states measured by EEG, studied in consciousness and sleep research. They are physiological measures, not a phenomenological feature of the experienced stream.
wrong.d: An oculomotor behaviour studied in perception, attention and reading research (eye tracking): an observable motor output indexing where attention points, not the stream's internally generated content.

q: ______ is a form of perspective taking that requires the ability to view a situation from at least two perspectives, that is to reason simultaneously about what two or more people are thinking.
who: Nested perspective taking (theory of mind)

concept.t: Recursive thought is precisely the perspective-taking ability to reason simultaneously about what two or more minds are thinking.

Perspective taking is the capacity to step outside one's own viewpoint and see how a situation appears to someone else. Recursive thought is a more advanced form that embeds one mental representation inside another: 'person 1 thinks that person 2 thinks that person 3 thinks'. A process operating on its own output is what makes the thought recursive.

It is the engine of a mature theory of mind, the understanding that others hold beliefs, desires and intentions different from one's own, and it underwrites complex social reasoning, deception and cooperation.

In Systems & Theories, it belongs to the developmental and cognitive lineage from Jean Piaget, whose stage theory of overcoming egocentrism and acquiring decentred, reversible reasoning was a pillar of the cognitive revolution that overthrew behaviourism in the 1950s-60s. Where behaviourism refused to theorize the inner mind, cognitive and developmental psychology made manipulating mental representations central. Theory-of-mind research (Premack and Woodruff; Wimmer and Perner's false-belief task) extended Piaget's foundation.
Recursive thought means holding at least two perspectives at once by embedding one mental representation inside another.

wrong.a: An early language-acquisition style (contrasted with expressive style) in which a toddler's first words are mostly object labels: vocabulary preferences, not nested perspective taking about other minds.
wrong.b: The Piagetian concrete-operational ability to mentally undo an action, which makes conservation possible. Same theoretical family, but it reverses physical transformations in one's own reasoning, not several people's thoughts.
wrong.d: Memory actively rebuilt at retrieval rather than replayed verbatim, a core finding of Frederic Bartlett's schema research. It describes how memories are reassembled; there is no embedding of one mind's view inside another's.

q: The current approach to psychology most closely aligned with the structuralists in its interest in topics like consciousness, mental imagery and thought process is:
who: Ulric Neisser's Cognitive Psychology (1967), heir to Wundt and Titchener

concept.t: Cognitive psychology revived the very topics, consciousness, mental imagery and thought, that the structuralists first studied.

Founded by Wilhelm Wundt and his student Edward Titchener, it tried to break conscious experience into basic elements using introspection, the trained self-report of one's own mental contents. It was psychology's first formal school after the discipline split from philosophy in 1879.

Functionalism (James, John Dewey) soon asked what mind is for. Then behaviourism under John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner rejected the study of mind entirely, examining only observable behaviour because inner states could not be measured objectively; for roughly forty years the mind was off-limits.

In the 1950s-60s, Ulric Neisser (whose 1967 Cognitive Psychology named the field), George Miller, Noam Chomsky's demolition of Skinnerian language and the new information-processing computer metaphor brought mental processes back to the centre. Cognitive psychology studies perception, attention, memory, mental imagery, language and thinking, but replaced unreliable introspection with rigorous experiments, reaction-time measures and models of a mind that encodes, stores and retrieves information. In Systems & Theories it is the heir that reclaimed structuralism's questions while inheriting behaviourism's experimental discipline.
Cognitive psychology matches structuralism in studying consciousness and thought, but uses controlled experiments rather than introspection.

wrong.a: Studies the brain's biological mechanisms (neurons, circuits, neurotransmitters, imaging): the physical substrate, not the structuralists' subjective mental elements. It often partners with cognition (cognitive neuroscience) but is not the closest match.
wrong.c: The school that rejected consciousness, imagery and introspection as unscientific and studied only overt behaviour: structuralism's direct opposite, not its heir.
wrong.d: Structuralism's contemporary rival (James, John Dewey, Angell), studying the purpose and adaptive function of mental processes, what mind does rather than what it is made of, so less aligned than cognitive psychology.

q: In the definition of Psychology, mental processes mean ________.
who: Covert mental processes versus overt behaviour

concept.t: In the standard definition of psychology, 'mental processes' denotes exactly the internal, covert processes.

Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes, a phrasing with two deliberate halves. Behaviour is everything an organism does that can be directly observed and measured from outside, such as speaking, walking or reacting. Mental processes are the internal events of the mind that cannot be seen directly (thinking, feeling, remembering, perceiving, dreaming, forming intentions), inferred from behaviour and self-report.
Covert means hidden or not openly displayed, the opposite of overt, meaning observable. The mechanism: we observe behaviour directly but infer mental processes from it.

In Systems & Theories, the two-part definition is a historical compromise. Early structuralism and functionalism studied the mind through introspection; behaviourism (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) stripped the definition to behaviour alone, banishing mind for decades; the cognitive revolution of the 1950s-60s (Ulric Neisser, Miller, and the information-processing model of a mind that encodes, stores and retrieves) restored internal events. The phrase fuses the behaviourist demand for observable action with the cognitive insistence that covert inner life is real and measurable through inference.
Mental processes are the internal, covert activities of the mind; behaviour is the overt, observable side.

wrong.b: The observable, overt half of psychology's definition, contrasted against mental processes. It is genuinely part of the same definition; picking the visible side when asked about the hidden side is the trap.
wrong.c: Observable behaviours, the precise opposite of covert mental processes: 'overt' literally means open and visible. The formal-sounding wording tempts, but it names the wrong half of the behaviour-versus-mind distinction.
wrong.d: A legitimate subject psychology studies (comparative psychology, learning research), not the meaning of 'mental processes', which are internal events in any organism, human or animal. Restricting the term to animals misreads the definition.

q: "The whole is greater than the sum of the parts and that the parts or subsystems are related to each other and to the whole" are emphasised in ________.
who: Ludwig von Bertalanffy, General System Theory

concept.t: The defining principle of systems theory is that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, and that the parts are interrelated with one another and with the whole.

A system is a set of interacting components forming an organized, unified whole. Systems theory, an interdisciplinary framework most associated with the biologist Ludwig von Bertalanffy and his General System Theory, studies how such systems behave across biology, organizations, families and psychology.

Its central claim is holism: a system cannot be fully understood from its parts in isolation, because their interactions produce emergent properties no single component possesses. Each subsystem relates both to the others and to the larger whole, so a change in one ripples through all.

In Systems & Theories, the idea has deep roots in Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Kurt Koffka, Wolfgang Köhler), whose slogan that the perceptual whole differs from the sum of its sensory parts opposed the element-by-element analysis of structuralism. Bertalanffy generalized it from perception to all organized systems in the mid-twentieth century; it later fed family-systems therapy and the move, contemporaneous with the cognitive revolution, away from reductionist behaviourism toward the organism as an integrated information-processing whole.
Systems theory is the framework defined by holism, interrelated subsystems and emergent wholes that exceed the sum of their parts.

wrong.a: Explains what energizes, directs and sustains behaviour (drives, needs, incentives): why organisms act, not the principle that interacting parts create emergent wholes.
wrong.b: The best course of action depends on the situation, with no universally best way; common in management and leadership. Its core is situational fit; nothing in it says the whole exceeds the sum of its parts.
wrong.d: Associated with Henri Fayol: principles of management and organizational structure (planning, organizing, commanding, coordinating, controlling). It concerns administering an organization efficiently, not systems holism.

q: The ________ framework is based on the expectancy, demand and incentive concepts.
who: Julian Rotter's social learning theory, extended by Albert Bandura

concept.t: The social learning framework explains behaviour through cognitive variables, notably expectancy, demand and incentive.

Developed by Julian Rotter and extended by Albert Bandura, it argues behaviour is shaped not by reinforcement alone but by how a person mentally interprets situations. A behaviour's likelihood depends on expectancy (belief about how probable an outcome is) and reinforcement value (how much that outcome is wanted, closely tied to incentive); demand is the pull of the situation and its goals. Combining these, the framework predicts choices from subjective cognition rather than purely external stimuli.

In Systems & Theories, it is the crucial bridge between behaviourism and the cognitive revolution. Classic behaviourists (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner) banned internal variables; neo-behaviourists (notably Tolman with his expectancies, and Clark Hull) reintroduced intervening cognitive constructs. Rotter and Bandura completed the move with expectancies, values and (in Bandura) self-efficacy and observational learning, helping carry psychology from stimulus-response into the mind-centred cognitive era of the 1950s-60s.

The printed key labels this the cognitive framework, and the listed concepts are indeed cognitive in nature. The keyed/intended answer here is social learning, but reason from how your specific paper frames it.
The expectancy-demand-incentive framework explains action through cognitive expectancies and the value of anticipated reinforcement, the hallmark of Rotter's social learning theory.

wrong.a: Explains action through observable stimulus-response links and reinforcement, deliberately excluding internal mental variables. Expectancy and incentive are internal interpretations that strict behaviourism rejects.
wrong.b: Covers thought, memory, attention and information processing; expectancy is genuinely cognitive and the printed key itself says 'cognitive'. However, the keyed answer gives the trio to social learning theory: treat it as a flagged debate.
wrong.d: Supportive models in organizational leadership and organizational behaviour stress managerial care, encouragement and backing of employees to build motivation and participation; nothing to do with Julian Rotter's expectancy-demand-incentive constructs.

q: The first major theoretical effort in information processing psychology was by ________ in the year ________?
who: Donald Broadbent, filter theory, Perception and Communication (1958)

concept.t: Donald Broadbent produced the first major theory cast explicitly in the information-processing mould.
The information-processing approach treats the mind like a system that takes in input, processes it through limited-capacity stages and produces output, much as a computer does.

Working on attention problems such as following one conversation among many (the cocktail-party problem, studied with dichotic listening), Broadbent proposed his filter theory in his 1958 book Perception and Communication. Information enters a brief sensory store, then a selective filter admits only one channel at a time based on physical features (which ear, what pitch). Because the filter acts before meaning is analysed, it is the early-selection view.

In Systems & Theories, the 1958 model is often treated as a founding landmark of the cognitive revolution that overthrew behaviourism. Drawing on wartime engineering, Shannon's information theory and the computer metaphor, it modelled the unobservable inner stages behaviourism had forbidden, alongside Miller's 1956 'magical number seven' and Chomsky's 1957 critique of behaviourist language. It directly seeded the flow-diagram models later popularized by Ulric Neisser.
Broadbent (1958) gave information-processing psychology its first major theory, the early-selection filter model: selective filtering at an early stage protects a limited-capacity channel.

wrong.a: Anne Treisman's attenuation theory (1960/1964) revised Broadbent, arguing the filter turns unattended channels down rather than fully off. Central to attention, but it came after the first major effort.
wrong.b: Noam Chomsky's 1957 Syntactic Structures was a linguistics landmark that fuelled the cognitive revolution, but it was a theory of grammar and critique of behaviourist language, not an information-processing model of attention.
wrong.d: John Watson (1920) founded behaviourism, which rejected modelling unobservable mental stages; information-processing theory postdates and opposes his approach.

q: Which approach of psychology, the main premise is that 'basically the behaviour of an individual is governed by the brain and nervous system'?
who: Neurobiological (biological) perspective: brain and nervous system

concept.t: The neurobiological approach holds that behaviour is fundamentally governed by the brain and nervous system.

Psychology has several broad perspectives, each explaining behaviour from a different angle. The neurobiological approach, also called the biological perspective, locates the causes of behaviour and mental processes in the body's physical machinery: brain, nervous system, neurons, neurotransmitters, hormones and genes. Every thought, feeling and action ultimately reflects underlying biological activity.

To explain behaviour you study how nerve cells are organized into functional circuits that process information and mediate action: a mood change might be traced to altered serotonin signalling, a memory deficit to hippocampal damage. It relies on brain imaging, lesion studies and physiological recording.

In Systems & Theories, it is one of psychology's oldest taproots, reaching back to René Descartes' mind-body problem and nineteenth-century physiology, the lab tradition (Helmholtz, Wilhelm Wundt's mentors) from which experimental psychology emerged in 1879. It ran in parallel through the behaviourist and cognitive eras, then fused with the cognitive revolution into cognitive neuroscience, mapping information-processing operations onto brain mechanisms: both a founding root and a current partner.

If a perspective says behaviour is fundamentally controlled by the brain and nervous system, explained through neurons and circuits, it is the neurobiological approach: neural and physiological events produce psychological outcomes.

wrong.a: Studies the lawful relationship between physical stimuli and sensations (Weber, Fechner) at the perceptual level, not neural circuitry controlling behaviour. 'Physical' and 'physiological' sound alike, which is the trap.
wrong.b: Focuses on internal information processing (thinking, attention, memory, language), treating the mind like a computer. Cognition explains behaviour through mental representations and information, not neurons.
wrong.d: Edward Tolman and Clark Hull's neo-behaviourism still centres on stimulus-response learning, adding intervening variables like drive or expectancy. It stays at the behavioural level rather than appealing to the nervous system.

q: Who proposed the 'Bottom-up process' theory of perception?
who: James Gibson, bottom-up direct perception (1972)

concept.t: James Gibson proposed the bottom-up, or direct, theory of perception.

Perception can be explained in two opposite directions. A bottom-up process starts with raw sensory data and builds upward in one direction, from simple features toward ever more complex representations, without relying on prior knowledge. A top-down process instead uses stored knowledge, context and expectation to interpret what the senses deliver.

Gibson (1972) called his bottom-up view direct perception. The environment itself supplies all the information a perceiver needs through the rich, structured pattern of light reaching the eye, the optic array, complete with affordances and invariant cues. So perception needs no inference or guesswork: the mechanism is direct detection of information already present in the optic array.

On the Systems & Theories map, the bottom-up versus top-down debate is central to the cognitive revolution, which modelled the mind as an information-processing system and asked how sensory input becomes meaningful perception. Gibson's ecological approach pushed back against the heavy computational, inference-laden models of cognitive psychology, insisting the information is in the world, not constructed in the head, with roots in the Gestalt emphasis on directly perceived structure. Richard Gregory's top-down constructivist account (perception as an active hypothesis built from past experience) instead extended Helmholtz's nineteenth-century 'unconscious inference.'
Gibson's bottom-up direct perception builds from raw sensory data, whereas Gregory's top-down theory relies on stored knowledge and inference.

wrong.a: Founder of Gestalt psychology, who demonstrated the phi phenomenon of apparent motion. Gestalt is about perception and shares Gibson's anti-elementarist flavour, but Wertheimer gave grouping principles, not the bottom-up direct-perception theory.
wrong.b: Hermann von Helmholtz proposed unconscious inference: perception built from rapid, automatic inferences using prior experience, an early top-down view. A towering perception figure, but he is the ancestor of Gregory's constructivism, Gibson's opposite.
wrong.d: The strongest distractor: Gibson's direct rival, always discussed alongside him. Gregory championed the top-down, constructivist theory (perception as an active hypothesis from stored knowledge and inference, extending Helmholtz), the exact opposite pole.

q: Who among the following studies how psychological processes may differ among people of different cultures?
who: Official key: social psychologists (stem describes cross-cultural psychology)

concept.t: The official key gives (c) social psychologists, although the stem (how psychological processes differ across cultures) is textbook cross-cultural psychology. The question preserves this debatable key.

It takes one process (conformity, perception, memory, attribution) and compares it across two or more cultural groups to expose how culture shapes it. Its working assumption, that mind is largely universal but culture produces real, measurable variation, is operationalised by Geert Hofstede's dimensions (individualism-collectivism, power distance).

Cultural psychology rejects that split: mind and culture are mutually constitutive and inseparable, so it interprets meaning inside a single culture rather than comparing across them. Social psychology, the keyed answer, studies how the real or imagined presence of others shapes an individual's thoughts and behaviour, usually within one society.

On the Systems & Theories map this partition matters because Indian psychology grew out of a reaction against culture-blind Western universalism. In the indigenization debate, Durganand Sinha argued that importing Western tests across cultures (the cross-cultural move) was not enough; India needed concepts grown from its own soil (Samkhya's gunas, the kosha model, yoga). Cross-cultural work compares; cultural and indigenous work build from within.

Comparing one psychological process between cultures to reveal cultural influence defines cross-cultural psychology, even where a key labels it social psychology. Knowing which of the three a question describes is the recurring trap.

wrong.a: They hold that mind and culture are mutually constitutive, so they study meaning within one culture and never compare across cultures. The stem's 'among people of different cultures' is comparison, the opposite stance.
wrong.b: The textbook fit for the stem (they compare the same process across cultures), hence tempting. Marked wrong only because this item's official key gives social psychology; treat the key as the debatable one.
wrong.d: The named subfields (cultural, cross-cultural, social) genuinely study cultural variation in behaviour, so at least one option fits and a blanket rejection cannot be right.

q: In Indian psychology, which of the following is NOT a component of Purusha and Prakriti according to Samkhya philosophy?
who: Kapila's Samkhya: Purusha is the passive, unchanging witness

concept.t: Describing Purusha as dynamic and ever-changing reverses the single most basic teaching of Samkhya, so (d) is the false statement.

Samkhya, one of the six classical darshanas (orthodox schools) of Indian philosophy, is traditionally credited to the sage Kapila. It is rigorously dualistic, positing two ultimate, independent, eternal principles. Purusha is pure consciousness, the eternal witness (sakshi): passive, attributeless, inactive, never changing, doing nothing but observing.

Prakriti is unconscious primordial matter, the cosmic substance from which everything material and even mental evolves. Its three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) rest in equilibrium until the mere proximity of Purusha disturbs them; Prakriti then unfolds intellect (buddhi), ego (ahamkara), mind (manas), the senses, and finally the Pancha Maha Bhutas (earth, water, fire, air, ether). Prakriti is the dynamic pole and Purusha the still one; liberation (kaivalya) is the discriminative knowledge that separates them.

On the Systems & Theories map, this Purusha-Prakriti split is the metaphysical backbone of Indian psychology: it grounds the gunas used to classify temperament, the kosha (sheath) model of the self, and Patanjali's Yoga, essentially Samkhya plus a method (stilling the mind so Purusha rests in its own nature). Where Western dualism (Descartes) pits mind against body, Samkhya pits consciousness against everything else, including mind, which is Prakriti.
Purusha is the still, passive witness-consciousness; Prakriti is the dynamic, evolving matter. Any statement flipping the two is the false one.

wrong.a: True: Prakriti genuinely is the primordial cosmic matter (mula-prakriti) from which all beings and the material-mental world evolve, so it accurately describes Samkhya and is not the exception.
wrong.b: True: Purusha is precisely defined as pure consciousness, the eternal witness, so this faithfully reports core Samkhya doctrine and is not reversed.
wrong.c: True: the Pancha Maha Bhutas, the five gross elements, are indeed among Prakriti's evolutes, produced as the gunas unfold.

q: Which Indian psychologist is known for contributing significantly to organizational behavior through the concept of nurturant task leadership?
who: Jai B. P. Sinha, Nurturant Task (NT) leadership

concept.t: JBP Sinha formulated the Nurturant Task leadership model, an Indian-psychology landmark.

Western leadership theory (Ohio State's consideration-versus-initiating-structure, Likert's participative systems, Blake and Mouton's grid) assumed workforces that prize autonomy, equality and self-direction. Jai B. P. Sinha, a leading Indian organizational psychologist, argued that typical Indian work culture is instead dependence-prone, status-conscious, personalised and familial, so imported participative models misfired.

The effective leader fuses a firm task orientation (clear goals, monitoring, demanding performance) with genuine nurturance (warmth, paternal care, concern for the subordinate's growth and wellbeing). Crucially the nurturance is conditional, given in proportion to the subordinate's effort, so affection and productivity reinforce each other. Sinha placed NT between the authoritarian and participative styles as a transitional optimum: the realistic best fit now, which can gradually move Indian workplaces toward participative management.

On the Systems & Theories map this is the indigenization project: build a model from the lived cultural psychology of the people studied rather than apply Western theory wholesale. It shares the spirit of Durganand Sinha's ecology-of-cognition work, and NT leadership is the organizational-behaviour flagship of the Indian psychology movement.
Nurturant task leadership = JBP Sinha: conditional warmth plus firm task focus, engineered for the Indian workplace, distinct from his namesake Durganand Sinha's deprivation research.

wrong.a: A major Indian psychologist of culture, self and the indigenization of psychology who co-edited important Indian psychology volumes. The NT model is not his; this confuses a culture-and-self theorist with an OB theorist.
wrong.c: Shares the surname and is the most famous indigenizer, but his work is on deprivation, the ecology of cognition and indigenization, not leadership. He is a different scholar from J.B.P. Sinha.
wrong.d: An experimental and perception psychologist at Patna, in the same milieu as JBP Sinha, hence credible. However he is associated with experimental and perceptual work, not Nurturant Task leadership, so wrong for an OB-leadership question.

q: In 1968, which of the following events significantly contributed to the development of Clinical Psychology in India?
who: Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP), founded 1968

concept.t: The Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP) was founded in 1968, and that founding is what ties the year to the discipline's growth.
Clinical psychology in India had to carve out an identity separate from general academic psychology (born at Calcutta in 1916) and from psychiatry (medical, hospital-based).

It gave the field its national professional home: it convenes practitioners, sets training and ethical standards, holds annual conferences and publishes the Indian Journal of Clinical Psychology. This institutionalisation turns a scattered set of practitioners into a recognised profession with a collective voice before regulators and the public.

On the Systems & Theories timeline, IACP belongs to the applied, professional strand, distinct from the academic-experimental strand (Sengupta, Calcutta) and the later indigenous Indian Psychology movement (Cornelissen, the 2002 Pondicherry Manifesto, the 2008 Handbook). Statutory regulation of clinical training came later through the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI), founded in 1992 and made a statutory body in 1993.
IACP, founded 1968, is the event that institutionalised clinical psychology as a distinct profession in India.

wrong.a: NIMHANS does have this unit and a long mental-health service history, but it is not tied to 1968 or to the profession's rise; it confuses a psychiatry-side service unit with the clinical psychologists' own body.
wrong.c: NIMHANS was indeed declared an Institute of National Importance, but in 2012 by an Act of Parliament, decades after 1968. The date alone rules it out.
wrong.d: The PsyD (Doctor of Psychology) is a much later North American, largely Western professional-doctorate model. Indian clinical training grew through M.Phil programmes regulated by the RCI, so it is wrong in time and place.

q: Which of the following Indian psychologists played a key role in establishing the first psychology laboratory in India?
who: Uma Chaudhuri per official key (lab usually credited to N. N. Sengupta)

concept.t: The official key credits Uma Chaudhuri with rooting early Indian psychological assessment at Calcutta and indigenizing a major projective test. The literal phrase 'first psychology laboratory' is more commonly tied to N. N. Sengupta, so the key is the debatable element.

Academic psychology in India began at Calcutta University, home of the country's first department and laboratory, where an experimental tradition took hold from 1916 under N. N. Sengupta. Building a psychology in India meant not only running labs but adapting Western instruments to work on Indian respondents, the core indigenization task on the Systems & Theories map.

Chaudhuri developed an Indian version of the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), a projective technique in which the person narrates stories about ambiguous pictures, projecting underlying needs, conflicts and motives (a method from Murray and Morgan's need-press theory). The original cards showed Western faces, dress and settings, which confused Indian respondents and distorted their stories, so she redrew them with India-specific figures and scenes. Such cultural adaptation separates mere importation of Western tools from a psychology grounded in Indian social reality.
The official key links Uma Chaudhuri to the Calcutta laboratory tradition and the India-adapted TAT, even though the very first laboratory is usually credited to N. N. Sengupta.

wrong.a: A respected theorist and author on the self, identity and the dialogue between Indian thought and Western psychology. That reputation makes him plausible, but he is not linked to founding the first laboratory or early test work.
wrong.c: India's best-known psychoanalyst, famous for cultural-psychoanalytic studies of Indian childhood, religion and sexuality. His work is interpretive and clinical-cultural, not laboratory founding or projective-test construction.
wrong.d: Girishwar Misra, a contemporary scholar of culture and self who edited major Indian psychology volumes, belongs to a far later generation than the 1916-era founding of the first laboratory; chronology alone excludes him.

q: Which of the following Indian psychologists played a key role in adapting the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) for the Indian social context?
who: Kamala Chaudhuri, Indian adaptation of Murray and Morgan's TAT

concept.t: Kamala Chaudhuri produced the Indian adaptation of the Thematic Apperception Test.
