The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) is a projective personality measure created at Harvard by Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan in the 1930s, grounded in Murray's need-press theory. The respondent invents a story for each ambiguous picture and, because the scenes are vague, unconsciously projects their own needs, drives, fears and key relationships into it, which the examiner then interprets.

The original cards showed American faces, clothing and surroundings, so Indian respondents found them alien and their stories grew thin and less revealing. Chaudhuri redrew the stimulus pictures with culturally appropriate figures, dress and settings mirroring Indian family and social life.

On the Systems & Theories map this is textbook test indigenization, the impulse that led Durganand Sinha to argue for an India-rooted psychology and Bhatia to build a non-verbal Indian intelligence battery. Adaptation matters because a projective test works only when the stimulus is ambiguous-yet-familiar; the wrong cultural cues confuse the respondent or pull culturally foreign responses, wrecking validity.
The original TAT belongs to Murray and Morgan; its Indian adaptation belongs to Kamala Chaudhuri.

wrong.a: A theorist of self and identity who bridges Indian philosophy and Western psychology, which keeps him in the Indian-psychology conversation. But he is a conceptual scholar, not a test constructor, and did not adapt the TAT.
wrong.c: He applied psychoanalytic interpretation to Indian culture, and the TAT's projective, depth-oriented nature makes him feel adjacent. Yet interpreting culture is not redrawing and standardising TAT cards; he did not produce the Indian adaptation.
wrong.d: The famous indigenizer of Indian psychology, so the natural decoy. His indigenization work was conceptual and on deprivation and the ecology of cognition, not this specific TAT adaptation, which was Kamala Chaudhuri's.

q: The Bhatia Battery of intelligence tests, widely used in Indian psychology, was developed by-
who: C. M. Bhatia, Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests (1955)

concept.t: The test bears C. M. Bhatia's name and he designed it for the Indian population.

Most standard intelligence tests (Binet, Wechsler verbal scales) were heavily verbal and depended on literacy and on English. A large share of the Indian population was illiterate and spoke many languages, so verbal tests gave invalid, unfair, culturally biased scores.

In 1955 Bhatia built the Bhatia Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence: fully non-verbal, performance-based, individually administered, needing no reading or writing. Its five subtests are the Kohs Block Design test (reproducing patterns with coloured cubes), the Pass-Along test, the pattern (Alexander) drawing test, an immediate-memory test and a picture-construction test. Instructions can be given by demonstration and responses are motor or visual, so it cuts across language and literacy barriers and remains a staple in Indian clinical and educational practice.

On the Systems & Theories map this is another indigenization node: an instrument fitted to Indian conditions instead of a Western verbal IQ test applied wholesale. The same logic lies behind the Indian TAT adaptations and the Indian psychology movement's insistence that tools fit the population they measure.
The Bhatia Battery, a non-verbal performance intelligence test built for India, was developed by C. M. Bhatia in 1955.

wrong.b: A culture-and-self scholar and editor of Indian-psychology volumes, not a psychometrician. He did not author the battery; the eponym itself rules him out.
wrong.c: The leading indigenizer, who worked on deprivation and the ecology of cognition, hence a plausible 'India-appropriate test' decoy. However his contribution was conceptual, not building the Kohs-based performance scale that carries Bhatia's name.
wrong.d: Famous for the Nurturant Task leadership model in organizational behaviour, a completely different domain. Leadership theory has nothing to do with a non-verbal IQ battery: a clear domain mismatch.

q: Which of the following psychologists contributed to the rise of Indian Psychology in the early 2000s and helped establish the Indian Psychology Institute?
who: Matthijs Cornelissen, Pondicherry Manifesto (2002) and Indian Psychology Institute

concept.t: Matthijs Cornelissen led the early-2000s revival of Indian Psychology and founded its institute.

Psychology in India means Western psychology practised by Indians (experimental labs, imported tests, mainstream theories). Indian Psychology (capitalised, as a movement) is a distinct system drawing its concepts from India's own traditions, the Vedas, Upanishads, Yoga, Samkhya, Vedanta and Buddhist thought. It puts consciousness and the nature of the self at the centre, rather than treating mind as merely behaviour or information processing.

After decades sidelined by Western dominance, these ideas revived around 2002. Cornelissen, a Dutch-origin scholar at the Sri Aurobindo Ashram in Pondicherry, helped organise the gatherings that produced the Pondicherry Manifesto on Indian Psychology (2002), a call for a psychology rooted in Indian thought. He founded the Indian Psychology Institute (IPI) at Pondicherry to advance teaching and research in consciousness-based, indigenous approaches.

On the Systems & Theories map this is the institutional rebirth of the indigenous strand, building on Sri Aurobindo's integral yoga and connecting to the 2008 Handbook of Indian Psychology. It goes further than Durganand Sinha's earlier indigenization (localising Western psychology) by deriving the framework itself from Indian metaphysics.
The early-2000s revival of Indian Psychology and the founding of the Indian Psychology Institute are associated with Matthijs Cornelissen.

wrong.b: India's celebrated cultural psychoanalyst, a magnet on any Indian-psychology question. His project is psychoanalytic interpretation of Indian culture, not the consciousness-based Indian Psychology movement, and he did not found the institute.
wrong.c: The towering earlier indigenizer, but chronology disqualifies him: Sinha died in 1998, before the early-2000s gatherings, the 2002 Manifesto and the IPI founding.
wrong.d: Writes deeply on the self and Indian thought and co-edited the 2008 Handbook, so he is part of the revival and a near-miss. But founding the institute is credited to Cornelissen at Pondicherry.

q: Which of the following correctly explains Prakriti in the Samkhya philosophy?
who: Samkhya's Prakriti (mula-prakriti), primordial matter of the three gunas

concept.t: In Samkhya, Prakriti is the primordial matter from which all forms of life emerge.

Samkhya, the dualistic Indian darshana, splits reality into two ultimate principles. Purusha is pure, passive, unchanging consciousness, the witnessing self that only observes. Prakriti is its exact opposite: the unconscious, primordial, material cause of the universe, often called mula-prakriti (root nature).

Prakriti is made of the three gunas, sattva (clarity, balance), rajas (activity, passion) and tamas (inertia, darkness), held in perfect equilibrium at rest. When the proximity of Purusha disturbs it, Prakriti unfolds the whole phenomenal world: physical objects and the five elements, and also the inner instruments buddhi (intellect), ahamkara (ego) and manas (mind). So Prakriti is dynamic and ever-changing while Purusha never acts; liberation (kaivalya) lies in discriminating the two.

On the Systems & Theories map, because mind itself is an evolute of Prakriti, Samkhya classifies cognition and personality as material and reserves only witnessing consciousness for Purusha. That cut is deeper than Western mind-body dualism and is the metaphysical root of the guna typology, the kosha model and Patanjali's Yoga.
Prakriti is the primordial, evolving matter that is the source of the physical and mental world; it is never the unchanging consciousness, which is Purusha.

wrong.a: The textbook definition of Purusha, the passive witness. This is the most common Samkhya swap, tempting because the two terms come as a pair; applying it to Prakriti reverses the doctrine.
wrong.c: Describes the immutability of Purusha, the still witness, remaining unaffected by change. Prakriti is by definition the dynamic, evolving principle whose disturbed gunas generate the whole world, so calling it unchanging confuses it with its opposite.
wrong.d: Again points to Purusha, the conscious witness-self. Subtle trap: buddhi (intellect) is an evolute of Prakriti, but Prakriti itself is the unconscious, insentient material cause, not a conscious self.

q: Which year marked the publication of the Handbook of Indian Psychology?
who: K. Ramakrishna Rao, Anand C. Paranjpe and Ajit K. Dalal (2008)

concept.t: The Handbook of Indian Psychology was published in 2008.

Indian Psychology as a movement builds psychology from India's own knowledge systems (Vedanta, Yoga, Samkhya, Buddhist thought) rather than importing Western frameworks. For decades these ideas circulated in scattered, uneven form, so the revival needed one authoritative reference to consolidate its concepts for a mainstream academic readership and give the field citable legitimacy.

It was edited by K. Ramakrishna Rao, Anand C. Paranjpe and Ajit K. Dalal and published in 2008 by Cambridge University Press (Foundation Books). Its chapters cover consciousness, the self, the gunas, yoga psychology, Buddhist psychology and indigenous concepts of wellbeing, presented with scholarly rigour against Western schools.

On the Systems & Theories timeline it is the textual capstone of the early-2000s revival, following the 2002 Pondicherry Manifesto and the founding of Cornelissen's Indian Psychology Institute. It turned a movement into a consolidated, teachable body of knowledge.
The standard trap is the cluster of nearby dates, so anchor two: Manifesto 2002, Handbook 2008 (Rao, Paranjpe and Dalal), six years apart.

wrong.a: Far too early: Western psychology then dominated Indian departments and the modern Indian-psychology revival had not coalesced. The consolidating Handbook capstones a movement that gathered force only around 2002.
wrong.b: Year of the Pondicherry Manifesto on Indian Psychology, the revival's founding declaration and call to arms. The consolidating Handbook came six years later, in 2008; mixing the two dates is the classic error.
wrong.d: Too late: the Handbook had already appeared in 2008. 2012 instead marks NIMHANS being declared an Institute of National Importance; choosing it may reflect confusion with that unrelated milestone.

q: Which term is best associated with Sattva, one of the three gunas in Indian psychology?
who: Samkhya's three gunas: Sattva, the guna of equilibrium and purity

concept.t: Sattva is precisely the guna of equilibrium and purity, so harmony and balance fit.

The gunas are the fundamental qualities or strands of Prakriti (primordial matter) in Samkhya philosophy. Everything material and mental is woven from three threads, always present together in differing proportions.

Sattva: purity, clarity, harmony, balance, knowledge, wisdom and goodness; when it dominates the mind is calm, lucid and discerning. Rajas: activity, passion, desire, restlessness and motion; it drives ambition and craving. Tamas: inertia, dullness, ignorance, darkness and confusion; it produces lethargy and delusion.

Their shifting balance shapes temperament, food preferences, mood and conduct, as elaborated in the Bhagavad Gita and the Samkhya Karika. On the Systems & Theories map the triguna is Indian psychology's native personality typology, like Western trait models but grounded in Prakriti and tied to the yogic goal of cultivating sattva and reducing rajas and tamas for self-realization (Patanjali's kaivalya). Modern Indian psychologists have built triguna inventories, an indigenization of personality measurement.
Sattva = harmony, balance, purity, wisdom; Rajas = passion and activity; Tamas = inertia and ignorance.

wrong.a: The defining marks of Rajas, the guna of activity, restlessness and craving, the energising, ambition-driving strand. The question asks for the harmonious guna, which is Sattva.
wrong.b: These describe Tamas, the guna of dullness, lethargy and delusion, the polar opposite of Sattva's clarity. Tamas darkens and stupefies the mind; Sattva illuminates it.
wrong.d: Again Tamas, the heavy, obscuring guna of delusion and inertia, restated in different words to double the Tamas decoy. It is the antithesis of lucid, balanced Sattva.

q: Arrange the following in temporal sequence: (a) Establishment of Psychology department in Mysore (b) Establishment of Psychology department in Calcutta (c) Establishment of Psychology department in Madras (d) Establishment of Psychology department in Pune (e) First Indian Journal of Psychology. Choose the correct option:
who: Calcutta 1916 (N. N. Sengupta), then Indian Journal of Psychology 1926

concept.t: Reading the events in time order gives (b) Calcutta, (e) Journal, (a) Mysore, (c) Madras, (d) Pune, which is exactly option (c) and matches the actual chronology.

The first Department of Psychology was set up at the University of Calcutta in 1916 by N. N. Sengupta, so (b) is earliest. Calcutta was the cradle of academic and experimental psychology in India: psychology's separation from philosophy into a laboratory science, the same Wundtian move that founded the discipline in the West.

Next the field got its first scholarly outlet, the Indian Journal of Psychology, in 1926, so (e) comes second. Departments then spread: Mysore (a, under M. V. Gopalswamy), then Madras (c), and later Pune (d).

On the Systems & Theories map this sequence is the skeleton of how the academic-experimental strand took root and diffused, before the later applied (IACP, 1968) and indigenous (Indian Psychology, post-2002) strands emerged.
The two dated anchors carry the whole answer: Calcutta department 1916 first, the Indian Journal of Psychology 1926 second, before the Mysore, Madras and Pune departments.

wrong.a: Starts correctly with Calcutta but puts both Mysore and Madras before the Indian Journal of Psychology, which is impossible: the Journal appeared in 1926, early in the diffusion.
wrong.b: A close decoy with the same Calcutta-first opening, but the Journal-versus-Mysore swap breaks it: the Journal (1926) came right after Calcutta and before Mysore.
wrong.d: Starts with Mysore and ends with the Journal, inverting both anchors: Calcutta's 1916 priority and the early 1926 Journal. The most clearly incorrect sequence.

q: Which university established the first Department of Psychology in India?
who: University of Calcutta under N. N. Sengupta (1916)

concept.t: The University of Calcutta established India's first Department of Psychology.
Academic psychology in India began as an offshoot of philosophy before becoming an independent experimental discipline, and that separation happened first at Calcutta.

In 1916 Calcutta founded the country's first independent Department of Psychology under N. N. Sengupta (Narendra Nath Sen Gupta), trained in the experimental tradition at Harvard (influenced by Hugo Munsterberg's lab). It was backed by the educationist and Vice-Chancellor Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee and the polymath philosopher Brajendra Nath Seal, whose mental-and-moral-philosophy syllabus had already seeded experimental psychology.

Establishing a dedicated department gave psychology its own laboratory, curriculum and faculty outside philosophy, so Calcutta is called the birthplace of academic and experimental psychology in India; Mysore, Madras and Pune came later. On the Systems & Theories map it marks the entry of the Western experimental tradition (Wilhelm Wundt's laboratory model), later challenged and complemented by the indigenous Indian Psychology movement drawing on Vedanta, Yoga and Samkhya.
The University of Calcutta, in 1916, under N. N. Sengupta, established the first Department of Psychology in India.

wrong.a: An important early department under M. V. Gopalswamy, who set up a psychology laboratory there, so a strong decoy. But it came after Calcutta: a major early centre, not the first.
wrong.b: Madras set up its department later and is generally counted as the second centre after Calcutta. Its genuine early importance tempts, but 'second, not first' is exactly why it is wrong.
wrong.d: Its department was founded well after Calcutta's pioneering 1916 department, late in the sequence. A recognisable name in Indian psychology, but with no claim to being first.

q: Who is regarded as the Father of Psychoanalysis in India?
who: Girindra Shekhar Bose, Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922)

concept.t: Girindra Shekhar Bose founded organised psychoanalysis in India and is honoured as its father.

Psychoanalysis was created in Europe by Sigmund Freud, but an indigenous pioneer led its transplantation to India. Bose, a physician and psychologist at Calcutta, established the Indian Psychoanalytical Society in 1922, the first psychoanalytic society outside the Western world, giving it an institutional base and affiliating it with the international psychoanalytic community.

He kept up a roughly two-decade correspondence with Freud, exchanging ideas and respectfully disagreeing. His most original contribution was opposite wishes: every wish coexists with its contrary, framed through Indian philosophical notions of paired opposites. He was thus a psychoanalyst of international stature from a non-Western setting.

On the Systems & Theories map Bose is the depth-psychology strand of Indian psychology and an early indigenization, reworking a Western depth theory through Hindu thought. Distinguish him from N. N. Sengupta, who founded academic experimental psychology at Calcutta, and from the later consciousness-based Indian Psychology movement (Cornelissen).
Girindra Shekhar Bose, founder of the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922) and Freud's correspondent, is the father of psychoanalysis in India.

wrong.a: Freud founded psychoanalysis itself, globally, so he is the most obvious lure. But the question asks for the father in India: Freud created the field worldwide, Bose rooted it in India.
wrong.b: Founder of modern experimental academic psychology in India (the 1916 Calcutta department): right era and country, wrong subdiscipline. Conflating Sengupta with Bose mixes the laboratory strand with the depth-psychology strand.
wrong.d: Founded the Mysore psychology department and its laboratory, an experimental contribution. A generic early decoy with no link to the Indian Psychoanalytical Society or depth psychology.

q: Which concept introduced by Girindra Shekhar Bose blended Hindu thoughts with Western psychology?
who: Girindra Shekhar Bose, Theory of Opposite Wishes

concept.t: The Theory of Opposite Wishes is the concept by which Bose wove Hindu thought into psychoanalysis.

Girindra Shekhar Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society (1922) and corresponded with Sigmund Freud for roughly two decades. He accepted much of the framework (the unconscious, conflict, wishes) but reworked it through an Indian philosophical lens centred on duality and paired opposites, a theme deep in Hindu thought (the play of complementary opposites, dvandva).

Every wish is accompanied by an equal and opposite counter-wish, so the psyche is structured around the coexistence and dynamic balancing of paired desires. This differs from Freud's model, in which repression simply holds a wish down, and it was the core of their friendly disagreement; Freud never fully accepted it.

On the Systems & Theories map it is the clearest example of indigenized psychoanalysis: a Western depth theory genuinely fused with Indian metaphysics, anticipating the later Indian Psychology movement's insistence on India's own traditions. Bose used Freud's universal concepts but did not originate them.
Bose's bridge between Hindu thought and Western psychoanalysis is the Theory of Opposite Wishes: every wish paired with its opposite.

wrong.a: One of Sigmund Freud's own core mechanisms (keeping unacceptable wishes out of awareness), so classical Western psychoanalysis, not Bose's India-specific innovation. Famous, but the Hindu-Western blend asked for is opposite wishes.
wrong.c: A moral or ethical dilemma from Indian philosophy (as in Arjuna's crisis in the Gita), genuinely Indian, which is the bait. It is not Bose's psychoanalytic contribution; picking it mistakes Indian-flavour for his specific theory.
wrong.d: Not a concept associated with Bose. Guilt features broadly in psychoanalysis (superego, conscience), so it sounds right, but no Bose theory of guilt integrates Hindu thought: a manufactured distractor.

q: In which year the first department of psychology in India was established?
who: Narendra Nath Sengupta, Calcutta's Department of Experimental Psychology (1916)

concept.t: India's first independent psychology department was founded in 1916.

Psychology in India first lived inside philosophy departments, so its emergence as a separate science is dated to one institutional event. In 1916 Narendra Nath Sengupta established the Department of Experimental Psychology at the University of Calcutta, the first independent psychology department in the country.

Sengupta had trained in the experimental tradition in the United States, and his department imported laboratory methods, the hallmark of scientific psychology since Wilhelm Wundt's 1879 Leipzig lab, giving the discipline its own faculty, syllabus and laboratory. The University of Madras followed as the second centre.

On the Systems & Theories map, 1916 anchors the academic-experimental strand, the entry of the Western laboratory paradigm. It later coexisted with the depth-psychology strand (Bose's 1922 society) and was eventually challenged by the indigenous Indian Psychology movement rooted in Vedanta and Yoga.

Watch the surrounding dates: 1916 is the department, 1922 is Bose's Indian Psychoanalytical Society, 1926 is the Indian Journal of Psychology. The first department was founded in 1916 at Calcutta by N. N. Sengupta.

wrong.a: Too early: psychology was still embedded within philosophy, so no independent department existed. A plausible near-miss just below the true year, but the separation came only in 1916.
wrong.c: A famous founding did happen that year, but it was G. S. Bose's Indian Psychoanalytical Society, not a department. Confusing the 1922 society with the 1916 department is the classic error.
wrong.d: Later than the actual 1916 founding and matches no key milestone; the next anchored events are 1922 (Bose's society) and 1926 (the Journal).

q: Among the following, which of the renowned figures is not associated with the inception of Academic Psychology in India?
who: Koneru Ramakrishna Rao, later Indian Psychology scholar, not a 1916 founder

concept.t: Unlike the others, Koneru Ramakrishna Rao was not part of the early founding of academic psychology in India.

Academic psychology in India was born at the University of Calcutta in 1916, tied to three figures. Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee, educationist and Vice-Chancellor, built up Calcutta University and backed the new discipline; Brajendra Nath Seal, professor of mental and moral philosophy, framed the early curriculum whose syllabus seeded experimental psychology. Narendra Nath Sengupta actually founded and ran the first Department of Psychology.

Rao belongs to a much later period: a parapsychologist, a leading theorist of the modern Indian Psychology movement and lead editor of the 2008 Handbook of Indian Psychology. On the Systems & Theories map he sits in the post-2002 indigenous-revival strand (consciousness studies, Vedantic and yogic psychology), a different chapter entirely.
All four are genuine, important Indian-psychology figures, so the discriminator is purely temporal-and-thematic: founders of 1916 versus a revivalist of the 2000s.
The inception trio is Mukherjee, Seal and Sengupta at Calcutta, whereas K. Ramakrishna Rao is a later Indian-Psychology scholar, not a founder.

wrong.a: True: Calcutta University's visionary educationist and Vice-Chancellor, instrumental in establishing the psychology department and giving it institutional support. Naming a real founder is the wrong choice in a NOT question.
wrong.c: True: as professor of mental and moral philosophy, Brajendra Nath Seal helped frame the early Calcutta curriculum from which experimental psychology grew, so he is a founder-era figure.
wrong.d: True: he founded the first independent psychology department at Calcutta in 1916, the most central inception figure. Selecting the actual founder reverses the truth completely, the clearest wrong answer.

q: Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP) was formed in the year-
who: Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP), founded 1968

concept.t: 1968 is the founding year of the Indian Association of Clinical Psychologists (IACP).

The IACP is the national professional association of clinical psychologists in India. A professional association formalises a discipline: it convenes practitioners, sets ethical and training standards, holds annual conferences and publishes scholarship; the IACP brings out the Indian Journal of Clinical Psychology.

Founding the IACP in 1968 gave clinical psychology a distinct collective identity in India, separate from general academic psychology (born at Calcutta in 1916) and from psychiatry (a medical specialty), plus a platform to advocate for the profession before regulators and the public.

On the Systems & Theories map it belongs to the applied-professional strand, between the early academic-experimental founding and the later statutory regulation of training through the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) (established 1992, statutory from 1993). The 1968 founding, however, is the key institutionalising event for the clinical field itself.
Do not drift to the surrounding 1970s dates: the IACP was founded in 1968 as the national body for clinical psychologists in India.

wrong.b: Just after the true 1968 founding, a typical off-by-two-years decoy; by then the IACP already existed. Its closeness to the correct year is what tempts.
wrong.c: After the fact: the IACP had been operating since 1968. Another near-miss in the early-1970s cluster, aimed at students who only vaguely recall 'late 1960s/early 1970s'.
wrong.d: A full decade off, well after the 1968 founding, and it matches no IACP milestone; the most clearly incorrect distractor.
